subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has dispatched a detachment from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to all jubilee and coronation celebrations beginning with Queen Victoria's diamond jubilee in 1897. In that year a detachment was included in the Canadian contingent, and the same action was taken at the coronations in 1902, 1911 and 1937. This year the Royal Canadian Mounted Police will provide a full mounted troop which will lead the Canadian contingent in the coronation procession. It will also provide a mounted escort for the carriage of the Prime Minister in order to conform to the practice to be followed by the prime ministers of the commonwealth. The force will also supply four mounts for the officers of the Canadian army forming the Canadian element of the Queen's commonwealth escort, and a mount for General H. D. G. Crerar, who will ride in the procession in his capacity as honorary aide-de-camp general to Her Majesty.
This year, in addition to the actual participation in the coronation parade, the troop is training as a musical ride, and has been invited to appear at the royal tournament at Olympia in the presence of Her Majesty the Queen. They will also appear 68108-1681
at some outstanding agricultural fairs in the United Kingdom. Just what engagements the troop can fulfil has not been finalized, but it is clear that there is a very considerable demand for its attendance, and it is proposed to accept as many engagements as can be filled between the date of the coronation and the return sailing date of July 7, 1953.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of Labour in connection with the grain handlers' strike on the Pacific coast. speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for having given me warning of this question.

Mr. Speaker, I think the position of the department should be stated. I presume that we have the largest staff of any department engaged in dealing with questions and orders for returns. I point out that this department was formed towards the end of 1950. Many of the questions go back far beyond that date, and I believe that applies to the orders for returns of the hon. member. The answers to these questions entail a good deal of research. We have buying officers in every part of Canada, in London and the United States. When we are asked about general purchasing, we have to get reports from all these agencies.
It is the policy of the department to give first priority to answering questions which come from the committee on defence expenditure. I think hon. members will realize that that is an active committee and entitled to get information just as fast as it can be prepared. The second priority is given to answering questions asked here in the house. We cannot do the impossible. In between answering questions and looking up data to prepare orders for returns, the senior members of our staff are required to carry on the day to day activities of the department. I may say that our department is not overstaffed and our responsibilities are heavy. It may be good fun for some of our junior members to pile questions on the order paper, and while they are entitled to their fun we can only do the best we can in answering them. We are doing just that. I cannot promise when the orders for returns will be answered.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, March 4, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.
(Translation):

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when I requested the adjournment of the debate at six o'clock last night, I was saying that the Canadian people will be rather poorly rewarded for redoubling their efforts during the last year since they are being asked to pay in taxes, during 1953-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-during the year 1953-1954, $335 million more than they paid during the fiscal year 1952-1953.
I	would now like to resume my speech by adding that, in my humble opinion, in order to reward the Canadian people the government should have avoided increasing the amount of taxes they will have to pay next year. I must add that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) did not apply the reductions in rates in the best possible places. For instance, the 11 per cent reduction in the individual income tax rate will benefit a class of people who are undoubtedly worthy of compassion and brings them a small measure of relief that will be welcome, but, just the same, the class of people to which it applies is not the poorest. There is another and even poorer class which would only be happy to be able to pay a little income tax. To that class of people, the minister has brought no relief whatsoever; I am referring to small labourers, farmers, at least small farmers, settlers, the sick, the crippled, and to all those who, for one reason or another, earn barely enough to feed themselves miserably and to dress and house themselves even more miserably. Still, it would have been possible to grant them some relief, by reducing the general sales tax which will yield next year, according to present forecasts, $590 million. A rate of 6 instead of 8 per cent, for instance, would have represented a saving
The Budget-Mr. Poulin of $150 million, and everybody would have benefited by it, the poor as well as the rich.
As a matter of fact, the public is wondering whether this budget will be the last before a general election.
Should this not be the case, I wonder if the Minister of Finance would not be well advised to lend an ear to my humble suggestion so as to implement it in his next budget which, of necessity, would be the last before the great adventure! Alternatively, there would be another measure with an almost similar effect and which would benefit everyone, or at least all those families with children-the very group which we should protect more than any other-and that would be to increase the family allowances to a level more or less proportionate to the rise in the cost of living we have experienced since this excellent social measure was introduced in this country.
And this brings me to say that, to my mind, the state does not give sufficient practical recognition to the importance of the part played by the family in our Canadian society. I can of course well imagine what some people will say to that: "But what of family allowances or income tax exemptions which increase with the number of children?" Now, it will be noticed, first of all, that I have not said that the state refused to recognize the part played by the family. I claim, however, that this recognition is not tangible enough.
Nowadays, every thinking person-thank God, there are still many, and fortunately even in our parliaments-wonders anxiously what means should be taken to provide the community with the well-trained subjects it needs so much. And yet, the answer is there, the machinery exists. It merely needs to be activated, improved and applied fully. This machinery, the only one which, to my mind, can be utilized, is the family to which the state should give all the necessary help and protection. The distinction is not sufficiently clear-cut in our fiscal methods, between families with children and those who have none or only a few; the former are in a state of inferiority compared to the latter. As the number of children increases, so does this disadvantage.
In the case of income tax, for instance, the amount of the exemption for each child is absolutely inadequate and illusory, and should be increased. Let us take, for instance, the case of a head of family who is the sole supporter of a household comprising a wife and
2638	HOUSE OF
The Budget

Mr. Poulin 5 children, or, sometimes, 8 or 10 children. Who will believe that family allowances or the lowering of income tax rates, if he pays income tax, will compensate for the amount he will have to pay in the form of excise tax or sales tax, since he has to foot the bill for 5, 8 or even 10 consumers? That, I believe, is a serious mistake which it is urgent to correct if the government wants to show that it really has faith in that sacred institution, the Canadian family.
In another chapter of his statement, under the title "Federal-Provincial Relations", the hon. Minister of Finance said, as reported at page 2130 of Hansard:
Of course the extent of federal taxes does make substantial tax increases by provincial governments more difficult. No royal commission is needed to discover this truth.
The minister was undoubtedly referring to the commission of inquiry just set up by the Quebec government.
The field to be covered by that commission is quite extensive. It will not limit itself to finding out whether it is difficult for Quebec to increase taxes further, as might be implied by the rather pungent innuendo of the hon. Minister of Finance.
That commission will inquire fully, at least I hope so, into the matter of fiscal relations between the federal government, the provinces and the municipalities; it should then be in a position to make suggestions acceptable to all concerned, which would precisely permit the correction of the present state of affairs.
Might it be, perchance, that the minister would want to limit the commission's field of activity? Would he have us believe that the province of Quebec must accept what has already been done and welcome any proposal made by the central power? If such is the case, the minister may have to sing a different tune one of these days.
The hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage), for whom I have much respect and whose talent I appreciate, has asked more than once since last year, of what taxation rights the federal government had deprived the provinces? The answer is that of course the federal government has not taken the rights themselves, since it cannot do so, but it has taken the taxes, the money, and that is the reason why the minister, whose worthy assistant he is, said in his speech that it would not be easy for Quebec to increase her own taxes. The federal gov-


ernment has not drained out the spring, but it has taken almost all the water, which amounts to the same thing.
Now, the minister having mentioned the Quebec royal commission on constitutional matters, it may be in order to quote here an appreciation which may be found in UAction Catholique for February 23, 1953, in an article entitled "Researchers worthy of their task", over the signature of Mr. L. T. Roy, editor-in-chief. I quote:
When the provincial government decided to implement the suggestion made by the chambers of commerce and to institute an inquiry into constitutional problems, there were some skeptics who doubted the seriousness of that suggestion. The act setting up the commission only reassured them to a limited extent. In other words they were waiting for the designation of the commissioners to form a definite opinion.
Now that these have been named, it is extremely difficult indeed not to find this choice excellent. Along with many others, this paper had expressed the wish that the persons chosen should be both competent and detached from politics. There is no possible doubt about the matter, this wish has been fulfilled.
With such commissioners the investigation into constitutional problems will most certainly be serious and the report which will result therefrom will no doubt be authoritative.
This at least holds out some hope that, at the next federal-provincial conference, if it is held, Quebec will have some concrete proposals to submit and its position will thus be strengthened.
There is no need for a royal commission, the minister said. Not any more, indeed, than there was need for the Massey-Levesque commission to establish a learned distinction between education and culture and to recommend that the central government should go still further in its encroachment upon the field of education. Not any more, I presume, than there was need for a Rowell-Sirois commission to recommend fiscal centralization.
No need for a royal commission? And yet, the federation of chambers of commerce of the province of Quebec came to Ottawa, on February 25 last, to remind the government that there would be one.
What is more, it told the Minister of Finance and the government that they should take its recommendations into account at the federal-provincial conference it has asked them to call.
However, Mr. Speaker, 1 would be unfair if I did not have a word of praise for the Minister of Finance, that is for the good and reasonable features of the budget he recently brought down.

For instance, I find excellent the tax credit allowed in respect of corporations operating in the provinces which have not signed a tax rental agreement with the federal government. Such a tax credit places corporations in our province on the same basis as those operating in other provinces and does away with a policy of discrimination. I thank the minister for that intelligent and commendable move, even if some smart people pretend to see in it a coarse appetizer placed on the table of the great electoral banquet which is near at hand.
As for the radio licence, it is a nuisance which is disappearing but I am not sure that this new 15 per cent tax on radios and their various components-tubes included if I am not mistaken-will not actually impose on radio users a financial burden which may equal or even sometimes exceed the amount of the former licence.
I also thoroughly approve of the discontinuance of stamps on cheques and other instruments. I must admit however that all this will profit but very little the farmer or worker with a small income. As I said at the outset, I am delighted with the 11 per cent income tax reduction; however, I contend that a more practical formula might have been adopted in this field. In my humble opinion, before granting this reduction-or better still, instead of granting it-the government could perhaps have raised the basic exemptions to $2,000 for the single person and to $3,000 for married men.
I also welcome the government's decision to grant a $400 exemption for each child over 21 who pursues special studies.

Besides, I indicated yesterday, I hope the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lesage) has not forgotten, the cuts that could have been made in order to grant relief to the Canadian taxpayer. I do not deem it necessary to go into that -.gain.
Besides, the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet, who is also parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, surprises me very much. Just now I offered him my best congratulations and I thought I had succeeded in drugging or chloroforming him, but I see that he is livelier than ever. Maybe he is one of those patients who are not easily put to sleep by anaesthetics, or maybe he is still in the early phase of anaesthesia which is called excitement phase.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Provincial anaesthesia?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can see no difference between provincial and federal anaesthesia.
Let us say, without malice of course and without labouring the point, that the budget would be worse without those features. I say "without labouring the point", because I know that the government's sympathizers will be more than apt to do the labouring.
And now, Mr. Speaker, before I conclude these remarks I want to say a few words on a subject which I believe comes under the authority of the Minister of Finance, the printing of bilingual old age pension cheques to be distributed everywhere in Canada.
Bilingualism is officially recognized in our country.
We already have bilingual money, not only in the province of Quebec, but everywhere in Canada. Objections were made at first but who dares complain now?
We are using bilingual stamps everywhere in the country. Has this done any harm? These past few years, family allowance cheques, and more recently, old age pension cheques have been bilingual, in the province of Quebec only. Has there been a single citizen in Quebec, out of four million people, to protest? Nobody in the province of Quebec-I insist on that point-has been offended because English words appeared on the cheques which have been distributed in that province, even though the French element represents nearly 85 per cent of the population. Why should citizens in other provinces be offended at the sight of French on their own cheques? Would that prejudice
2640	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Poulin someone in any way, except perhaps a few employees who, through fanaticism and intransigence, are tarnishing the reputation of tolerance and broadmindedness of which the vast majority of the Canadian people, whatever be their racial origin, are justly proud.
Those responsible for such a state of affairs should remember that there are more than four million citizens of French origin in Canada, including one million outside Quebec, who are entitled to treatment equal to that given Canadians of English origin.
It seems evident that in our country, where two great races are intermingled and are called upon to live side by side, where there is neither victor nor vanquished, it is desirable that there be an atmosphere of mutual confidence and respect. In my humble opinion, such confidence and respect cannot [DOT]exist unless each of our two great races gives to the other all possible means of enjoying fully its rights and privileges.
This is an excellent occasion for the most numerous ethnical groups in this country, as well as for the government, to grant to one of those two races the enjoyment of a right- and not a privilege-which would entail no sacrifice whatsoever for the other group and not the least difficulty for the government.
Truly, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, why should it be more difficult for the government to issue bilingual cheques than for the Bank of Canada to issue bilingual notes? As a matter of fact, there is no such difficulty, because the cheques for the province of Quebec are already printed in both languages. All that is necessary to implement that recommendation is a little understanding and good will, of which, fortunately, increasing examples are to be found among the majority group in Canada.
And not only pension cheques, but all cheques issued by each and every department of the federal government should be bilingual.
This is, in my humble opinion, an opportunity for this government to correct a situation which is abnormal in a country like ours.
This might also give the Minister of Finance food for thought. I know he is intelligent, extremely gifted and well intentioned. He is from the province of Quebec and consequently, even though I hardly expect from him an immediate reaction, I am convinced that, deep down, he must admit the reasonableness of my request. In any event, he sets us an example since he is himself perfectly bilingual. It is said of him that he might possibly, some day, become the Liberal party leader. Such being the case, the prov-

ince of Quebec could not help but be grateful to him were he to make this gesture, inspired by the most genuine Canadian patriotism.
Consequently I have no doubt that it will be agreeable and possible for the government to lend an attentive ear to my humble suggestion, a suggestion which I have put to him at the request of several thousand citizens of the constituency of Beauce which I have the honour of representing here.

Mr. Speaker, there are several matters I should like to discuss in this budget debate, but before doing so I will make a few observations about comments already made by other hon. members who have spoken. I would refer first of all to some examples given on February 27 by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore). As reported at page 2465 of Hansard he made reference to the married man with two dependents and earning $2,400 a year, and stated that this taxpayer is paying only $15.
In the first place that is wrong because the hon. member, had forgotten the 2 per cent social security tax, which brings this man's tax up to $17. However, I do not know that I would stress that as an objection to his observations. The particular exception I take is to the word "only". Particularly is this so when the treatment received by this man is compared with that received by another man in the same circumstances-married with two dependents-and with an income of $10,000, received entirely from investments. This man would pay nothing, not even the social security tax, because on the $10,000 he would have a tax of $1,582, and he would then add $60 as social security tax, bringing the whole tax up to $1,642. May I comment at this point that the 2 per cent tax would be $200, of course, if the whole amount were applicable. But because of the ceiling of $60 having been placed thereon, he would be charged only at that rate.
Even so, the 20 per cent rebate on dividends given to him not only completely wipes out this amount of indebtedness, but would allow him to make even more than $10,000 before he would have any tax whatever to pay.
In this connection I should like for a moment to refer to some observations made by the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) the other afternoon when, referring to this provision, he said:
-there must be very few taxpayers, if any, whose tax liability would be cancelled by the 20 per cent tax credit on dividends.

Well, as the hon. member says, there may be very ffew. But according to the figures of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) presented in his budget speech there is $20 million worth of tax relief given to people whose incomes are from dividends paid by tax-paying Canadian corporations.
It would seem to me therefore that if this relief can be given to these people, then it should have been possible to give at least some measure of relief to those in the lower income brackets by way of increased exemptions, or it should have been possible to do something in respect of medical expenses. I shall make further reference later to medical expenses but, at the moment, I should like to revert to what was said by the hon. member for Vegreville. He made further reference to a man with a wife and two children, having an income of $3,000, and estimates his tax at $205. I think perhaps he did not say that, because the actual amount is $105. I would suppose that is an error in printing. But, of course, to the $105 he would still have to add his social security tax of 2 per cent, or $14, bringing the amount up to $119.
True enough, the man who makes $3,000 would probably receive family allowance payments for children amounting anywhere from $120 to $192 a year, depending upon the age of the children.

The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend a little time on some of the'omissions from the budget. I will deal first of all with medical expenses. As this house knows, I have been interested in this matter for some time. I do not believe that the slight nod which the government made in the direction of the taxpayer is going to benefit him to any marked degree. I would like to draw attention to the fact that there is the same deduction for medical expenses whether the taxpayer is married, single, or married with other dependents.
If the government was not willing to wipe out the 4 per cent floor it could at least have applied that 4 per cent on the taxable income rather than on the net income as at present. In the case of a single man this would mean, with a salary of $3,000, instead of a $120 floor for medical expenses he could deduct his statutory exemption of $1,000 and calculate his medical expenses on the remaining $2,000 and have an $80 floor. However, when it comes to the case of married people and people with dependents the situation would improve to some considerable degree. Take the case of a married man with a salary of $3,000. Instead of a $120 floor he would have a $40 floor, calculated on his taxable income of $1,000. If he happened to have two children dependent on him, instead of that $40 floor he would have a $28 floor, and so on.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that would have been a much more practical approach to the problem than the approach which the government took, merely taking off 1 per cent. That, as I said before, is nothing more than a friendly nod in the direction of the taxpayer and one that I doubt he is going to return with any degree of warmth.
There is another aspect with respect to these medical expenses which I believe has been overlooked. It is the problem which I mentioned last year of those who have in any year lost a dependent and who are now faced with the cancellation of that dependent's allowance and also with ^ the accrued debts which they must pay. This is particularly true of those persons who are now classified as single persons and who were formerly classified as married persons- who have lost $1,000 additional exemption from income for tax purposes. Here they are now with a $1,000 exemption instead of $2,000 which they had formerly. They are saddled with the debts which have accrued during the illness of their beloved person and they also have funeral expenses. The reduction in the exemption in itself makes them liable for another $150 basic tax plus another $20 social security tax. In other

The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough words, they have an additional $170 tax on account of the lost exemption alone.
They have their accrued medical bills, their accrued hospital bills and funeral expenses.
I might point out one thing here, and it is that in spite of the fact they still have the bills to pay they cannot claim them as medical expenses at all because they are no longer for a dependent. You can only claim medical expenses on behalf of a dependent.
I think that the law should be changed to permit claiming for medical expenses for say two years after the demise of the dependent -provided	the payments are properly
vouched and that it can be proved that they applied to the dependent who has been lost.
There is still another aspect of medical expenses which should be investigated, and it is the matter, in these days of very high costs of hospital and medical services, of exemptions for those persons who contribute toward the cost of such services to members of their family who are not direct dependents. There are people I know who pay hospital and medical expenses for parents, for brothers and sisters, for nieces and nephews, for uncles and aunts who are not actually dependents of the taxpayer. Because they cannot properly be classified as dependents, the taxpayer is prohibited from claiming these expenses as a deduction from his income tax.
It would seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is a very desirable thing that those people who are able to help their relatives who are not well off should be encouraged to do so.
I would urge upon the government consideration of this problem and suggest that they seriously go into the matter of permitting these deductions from income tax on the part of anyone who can produce vouched proof of their expenditure on behalf of relatives who are not dependent upon them, but on whose behalf they have paid medical bills. After all we do allow charitable deductions to the extent of 10 per cent of net income, and I might say, Mr. Speaker, that there is an age old adage that charity begins at home. There is also another saying that blood is thicker than water, and it seems to me that the government might very well take cognizance of the fact that these people have a duty to perform to those less fortunate than themselves, and they should not be discouraged from performing that duty by a failure on the part of the government to recognize that responsibility.
I should like also to speak for a few minutes about the situation which was raised by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) in his official criticism of the budget and on which he did not speak at (Mrs. Fairclough.]

any length. I recall that he said municipalities cannot be ignored any longer. With this, Mr. Speaker, I could not agree more heartily. I do not have time in this short debate to go into the ramifications of the cost of housing, the burden which local improvements place upon that cost, the charges for welfare, hospitalization and such like, which are borne entirely by real estate within the municipalities today.
I only wish to repeat that which I have said on former occasions, and to agree with the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) in the plea that those requirements of the municipalities which are presently subject to sales tax should be exempted from that duty. It seems to me this is a very small way in which the federal jurisdiction could take cognizance of the plight of the municipality and assist to a small degree in the alleviation of the distress which the municipalities are suffering at the present time without upsetting jurisdictional balance.
Surely for an administration which takes 71.7 per cent of the tax dollar, as the official critic of this party has indicated, there might be some recognition, at least, of the plight of the municipality to the extent of allowing them the exemption from sales tax on their own purchases which they seek. After all, except in rare cases the dominion government does not pay any taxes to the municipalities for the premises which they occupy; and while they are ahsolved from this levy, they nevertheless practise a Scrooge-like policy in the strict accounting for sales tax on a great many of the supplies which are necessary to the life of the municipality.
In the city of Hamilton, this would amount to about one-third of a mill on the tax rate because, I am informed, the sales tax paid by the city of Hamilton to the federal government is in excess of $100,000, whereas the total assessment is some $365 million. This in itself would be a matter of some considerable relief to the hard-pressed taxpayers of the city of Hamilton who pay not only their federal income tax and their indirect taxation in the form of sales tax and other levies but also the taxes on the dwellings which they occupy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, while it is true that the government has given relief to small corporations, I should like to draw their attention to the fact that there are still a large number of small businessmen in the category of nonincorporated business, proprietorships or partnerships, who have not received any relief whatever except the small concessions which have been made to the individual taxpayer under this budget. If there is one class of

taxpayer in this country which has suffered throughout the years by reason of the high taxation imposed upon business, it is the proprietor of the small business who is in the non-incorporated category. Whether he withdraws his earnings or leaves them in the business for expansion, nevertheless he is subject to personal income tax on the total profits of his business. I have long felt that some concession should be made to this category of taxpayer, by making provision for those profits which are reinvested in the business through the purchase of additional plant, and equipment.
There are several other matters, Mr. Speaker, which I should like to mention. First of all, I should like to make a few remarks about depreciation. Generally, so far as accountants and businessmen are concerned, the government's move to the reducing balance method of depreciation has been extremely unpopular. This plan involved the division of depreciable assets into classes which were sometimes poorly defined, and also provided for the recapture of depreciation at the end of the period of ownership of the various classes of fixed assets. The scheme was supposed to save much work, but it has not been practical and to most taxpayers it has meant more work instead of less work, as well as considerable confusion. Furthermore it violates accepted business principles in providing for excessive depreciation rates in certain years, and in not permitting full depreciation until disposal of all assets in a class, requiring that depreciation be set out on the books of the taxpayer before being allowed, and so on. Moreover, it has actually placed a tax on capital appreciation and capital gains arising from the recent inflationary price rise. I think that is a very important matter, and one which should be considered, because it has been the government's avowed intention not to tax capital gains. When new fixed assets are being acquired, the higher prices of today must be paid and yet the taxpayer is required to pay a tax on recaptured depreciation which he badly needs to help him finance the new asset.
I should like to speak also about what is deemed to be dividends. In the case of a company which elected to pay a tax on its undistributed income on hand in accordance with section 95A 2(b) of the Income Tax Act, and has declared a dividend to permit it to do so, there is a necessity to first calculate the undistributed income on hand itself. It would be some time before the government assessors would check this calculation and
The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough verify or amend it. It is a fact that a number of companies have calculated a larger figure than was subsequently determined as acceptable to the assessors-sometimes quite a bit more. If the estimate of the corporation turned out to be in excess of the amount assessed by the government auditors, then a dividend had been deemed to have been paid beyond that envisaged by the section. Nevertheless, having been obliged to leap before it could look clearly, a company should have been in a position to make this situation right by having the dividend paid recognized as similar to what was later approved as the correct amount, so that the excess dividend paid could be used up in a way available to the company on earnings after the 1949 fiscal period. The wording of the act and the attitude of the government auditors is that any excessive amounts so paid in unavoidable error is deemed to be regular dividends and the full amount of the tax must be paid upon them by the shareholders with no counterbalancing allowance for a distribution of income at a cost of 15 per cent. No recourse will be allowed by the payment of a 15 per cent tax on an equal amount. This places the shareholders in a position which has cost them considerably more tax beyond that which would have been payable by taxpayers who were able to calculate the payment of a dividend which agreed with the interpretation of government assessors at a later date. Undoubtedly, Mr. Speaker, the companies should be equipped with crystal balls or some such devices for trying to ascertain at just what point the government assessors and auditors will agree with their own calculations. Some provision should be introduced into the act, or probably recognized in the regulations, to remove the inequity in cases of this sort.
There is also the matter of the tax on certain stock redemptions. There have been some serious cases of impropriety in the taxing of stock redemptions when a part of the redemption price represented an excess over the original paid-in value of the stock. I should like to cite a couple of cases, Mr. Speaker. There is the case of the St. Lawrence corporation which was well publicized in the Financial Post of November last. Many persons who purchased shares of that company on the open market before they were to be redeemed found themselves taxed on the premium even though they realized only a small part of it personally or perhaps none at all. They had no knowledge when they purchased the shares of the vending party that there could be a very substantial tax to pay as a result of the purchase. If they

The Budget-Mrs. Fairclough were found liable for the tax, it was determined at a later date and they were assessed without recourse. Another example could be the case of Loblaw "A" shares which are redeemable at $50 per share, although the paid-in value is about $3 or $4 each. A holder at the present time who has held the stock from its early days can cash in on the substantial premium now by selling the stock on the open market, and a purchaser at the present time may find that he will have a substantial loss on the stock if the company decides to redeem it at the $50 price with the resulting heavy tax liability which will then accrue to the holder. Some scheme should be worked out to mitigate this trouble. Possibly the government could see its way clear to allow a capitalization of this premium and a payment of a 15 per cent tax thereon as the only tax, the same as is done now under section 95A of the Income Tax Act.
There is also the matter of the receipt of bond interest. After I had made a few notes on this matter, I was interested in noticing, in the expressions of opinion given by leading businessmen of Canada, that one of them had remarked on this very matter of the taxation of bond interest in the hands of those persons who receive bond coupons on the full amount of the interest income that the coupon represents, even though the present owner may have paid a substantial part of the value of that interest coupon to the vendor at the time he bought the bond. Nevertheless, he is assessed on the total amount. The vendor receives his interest tax free if he does not wish to report it as income, whereas the purchaser pays income tax on more revenue than he actually earned. If, however, the vendor is fair about his earnings and reports accrued interest, calls it income in his own hands, nevertheless the purchaser is still taxed and the government collects tax twice on the same bond interest: once on the vendor because of his own declaration of income and again on the purchaser when he cashes his coupons. It would seem to me that this is another matter that should be corrected in the act and in the regulations, and in government policy.
I know several representations have been made to the department on behalf of selfemployed persons and those people in the professions who wish to provide for their own retirement by purchase of pensions or purchase of annuities of some sort or another. This is another matter which came to my mind with regard to omissions in the budget. There is quite a need for the government to give to self-employed persons the same beneficial tax treatment which it accords to those 

people who participate in pension and retirement plans through their employers, frequently large corporations. I do not think it should be a difficult thing to work out some equitable arrangement within the framework of the Income Tax Act, but no indication has been given that the government intends even to consider this matter. I think it is an inequity. It is a matter which should be taken under serious consideration by the government. It is a situation which should be corrected.
I should like to say a few words with regard to sales tax, quite apart from those remarks which I made about sales tax now paid by municipalities. It is, of course, a hidden tax, Mr. Speaker, and it tends to pyramid in the price of goods, often several times, before they reach the ultimate consumer. I know this matter has been discussed in this house on other occasions. I know that this same remark has been made before. But we should realize that the sales tax affects the man in the lower income tax bracket or the man who pays no income tax at all much more than it affects any other class of taxpayer. A reduction in the sales tax might, I think, have been considered when the government was considering where it should distribute its favours. I also think that if and when a reduction in sales tax is made, it should be accompanied by pointed government comment that it be passed on to a reasonable extent at least to the consumer. If this were done, the result would be to make the job of balancing the family budget a little bit easier at the very time when it seems to be almost impossible to make a family's expenditures keep down to the level of the family income.
There are other matters of tax inequalities which I should like to mention. One in particular is with regard to succession duty. The government has been told frequently about the inequity which exists in the Dominion Succession Duty Act respecting duties levied thereunder on estates which have a total value slightly in excess of $50,000. No tax is charged up to $50,000 but rates start above that amount; and there is in the act a provision which states that if any duty would reduce the estate below $50,000, then only the excess over $50,000 will represent the amount of tax owing. This means, Mr. Speaker, that an estate of $50,000, $51,000 or $52,000, and sometimes more, will still net only $50,000 to the beneficiaries. This means that there is in reality a tax of 100 per cent on a certain bracket of estate valuation which ordinarily would be subject to a

very small rate, and there is a distinct inequity to taxpayers whose estates have totals in this area.
Mr. Speaker, I admit that these remarks have been rambling but 1 am sure the house will realize that these are specific items which I wish to draw to its attention. In closing I should like to say this. There is little logical reason in support of the government's schemes in the last few years of using the income tax as a tool to achieve certain economic results. In particular, they have used the regulations on accelerated depreciation and deferred depreciation for this effect. The regulations create concealed subsidies in the case of accelerated depreciation, or concealed penalties in the case of deferred depreciation; and in either case, they are of uncertain amount and of rather uncertain effect upon the populace. The benefits and penalties fall unevenly on the taxpayers who, across the country, are taxed at widely divergent rates. Certain persons who are meant to be encouraged by accelerated depreciation allowances may not find that the monetary results are worth while; whereas other persons for whom the benefit is not meant may take advantage of it. Conversely, the penalties of deferred depreciation are unequal and do not always fall upon the persons most requiring them. The effect upon the government revenue is also concealed and actually unknown. It would be better for the government, if it meant to encourage business and capital expenditures, to pay a more direct form of subsidy or to give a definite dollar credit against taxes; or, in the case of deferred depreciation, to penalize or discourage the proper taxpayers with a definite ascertainable dollar value of penalty.
The government might claim that the regulations did not force an individual to take depreciation on his books on the same basis as he is claiming for tax purposes. I know that has been said before. But this ignores the fact that most small businesses wish to keep their books in line with the depreciation reserves which are set up by the income tax department, so as not to confuse matters by having two schedules, one for the books and another for the government.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that for too long a time the government has used income tax as a tool, to achieve certain economic results, which has not proved at all to the satisfaction of the taxpayer.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. Dickey (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in entering this debate I should like first of all to congratulate the Minister of
The Budget-Mr. Dickey Finance (Mr. Abbott) not only on the excellent budget which he presented to the house in moving this motion, but also on the truly exceptional manner of its presentation. If it is true that practice makes perfect, the experience the minister has had in delivering the seven budget speeches which preceded this one has certainly done its work. His presentation on this occasion was as close to perfection as anything that could have been wished. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that this occasioned us no surprise. The reaction of the official opposition to the budget has, however, given rise to some real surprise. The attitude taken by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the chief financial critic, amazed us for two reasons. I may say that his attitude has been followed by other members of his party who have participated in this debate.
The first cause for amazement was the fact that the hon. member for Greenwood chose virtually to ignore the budget and its provisions. Strange as it may seem, this is undoubtedly a compliment. The hon. member's purpose in discussing the budget would be only to find fault with it; and the meagre amount of time that he devoted to it indicates his inability to discover substantial grounds for criticism.
The other surprising facet of his position is the fact that the burdens of his small criticisms of the budget are that it is a rich man's budget. The incongruity of the financial critic of the Tory party taking a position of this kind has been drawn to attention by a number of speakers who have preceded me in this debate. There is one aspect of this situation, however, with which I feel I might deal very briefly. In order to recognize the shallowness and insincerity of the arguments that have been presented to try to label this budget a rich man's budget we have only to look at the record.
This argument is of course based on the budget's proposals in connection with the personal income tax. All hon. members will recall that as a result of a series of downward changes completed in 1948 and 1949, the rates of personal income tax in Canada were reduced to a point far below their wartime peaks. We had achieved at that time what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) described as a tax structure which was a well balanced blend designed to be simple and flexible, and one that could be readily adapted by moderate changes in rates to meet any reasonable scale of peacetime requirements.
Hon. members will also recall the cries of anguish with which the Minister of Finance's budget proposals were greeted by the official

The Budget-Mr. Dickey opposition in March, 1949. The cry was at that time that the rates of personal income tax which were being adopted amounted to a bribe to the electorate. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, as the chief financial critic then was before he became a displaced person, only to return to us as the member for Greenwood, cried out to the minister admonishing him at page 1810 of Hansard for March 22, 1949, not to imagine that:
. . . we are so stupid as not to realize the trick which you have tried to play on us.
He said further, at page 1808 of Hansard:
I hope you will let me know, Mr. Speaker, whether the word I intend to use is parliamentary, and if it is I would think that we are not wrong in calling this a bribery budget.
These charges of pandering to public demand for lower and more reasonable taxes and bribing the people with their own money were applied by the hon. member and the other members of his party to the income tax rates established for Canadians by the Minister of Finance in 1949.
As hon. members will recall, in June, 1950, the Korean war broke out. Parliament met in early autumn of that year and again in regular session during the winter of 1951. In two successive budgets the Minister of Finance found it necessary to impose sharply increased rates of taxation on the Canadian people to meet the extraordinary and rising costs of defence. One of the most unpleasant parts of this program of increased taxation .was the imposition of a 20 per cent surcharge across the board on personal income tax. This was a blow to the people of Canada, but one to which they responded loyally and in a most responsible manner. The opposition cry now was overtaxation, and we were accused of bleeding the Canadian nation. In spite of these prophets of doom the Canadian economy prospered and waxed strong, and by the time the Minister of Finance rose in his place in this house on April 8, 1952, to deliver his seventh budget speech he was able to say at page 1253 of Hansard:
In the personal income tax field a new rate schedule will be introduced. Into this new schedule I propose to incorporate most of the weight of the present 20 per cent surcharge. There will be some over-all abatement, although I should remind the house that the 2 per cent income tax imposed by parliament last session under the Old Age Security Act will be coming into force on July 1 of this year.
In so far as the rates of personal income tax are concerned the Minister of Finance at that time was able to remove one-third of the impact of the 20 per cent surcharge levied after the outbreak of the Korean war. This year a continued improvement in Canada's prosperity has permitted a further


reduction in taxation. The Minister of Finance has taken advantage of this opportunity completely to remove the remainder of the 20 per cent surcharge imposed in 1951 and has recommended the re-enactment of the identical rates of personal income tax which were in effect as a result of his budget proposals in 1949. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the very scale of personal income tax which in 1949 was described as a bribe to the Canadian people, and was derided by my hon. friends opposite as a trick to win an election, is now by those same hon. members being labelled as a rich man's budget. Incongruous? Obviously! Inconsistent? Definitely! Once again, Mr. Speaker, they want it both ways. They wish to represent the government at one time as bribing the people with their own money, and yet when the identical rates of taxation are again re-enacted they claim it is a rich man's budget.
I now wish to turn, Mr. Speaker, to. another matter of importance. In view of the fact that there has been a considerable amount of rather vague and general criticism of the construction work which is being performed for the Department of National Defence on what is broadly termed a cost-plus basis, it might be well for me to deal with this particular aspect of our construction program in some detail at the present time. This will of course be in addition to any consideration that the committee on defence expenditure may care to give to the subject when the committee reaches the general subject of construction. Perhaps I should say first of all that construction to meet the needs of the Department of National Defence and certain other defence agencies is the direct and full responsibility of the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), the sole exception being married quarters provided for military personnel.
A crown corporation known as Defence Construction Limited has been set up to oversee this program, and the corporation reports to and is responsible to the Minister of Defence Production. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation acts as agent for Defence Construction Limited in carrying out certain of the supervisory and overseeing functions required for the construction program, but in a general way it is correct to say that the execution of the construction program-including the letting of contracts, inspection and overseeing-is performed by agencies reporting in this respect to the Minister of Defence Production.
In the placing of contracts for all construction required for defence, the general and almost universally adopted principle is to invite competitive tenders by public

advertisement and to award a fixed price contract to the lowest tender received. This basic principle is adhered to with the greatest possible strictness and in every case where this proves to be possible. The policy of calling competitive public tenders is I think recognized in most cases as one of the most effective ways to ensure that work is done at the lowest possible cost. There are, both in civilian and defence construction, instances where the policy of a firm price contract resulting from a public call for tenders simply cannot be followed. In the inflationary period following the end of world war II it became very difficult for construction contractors to estimate the cost of labour and materials for projects requiring a year or more to complete. It therefore became 'common practice in industry for construction work to be carried out either on a "cost-plus" or "escalator" basis with "cost-plus" being most common in the case of large projects involving an expenditure of a million dollars or more. At a time when the trend seemed to be going back to keener competition and firm prices, the war in Korea broke out, heralding a new period of uncertainty accompanied by shortages of construction materials, particularly those having large steel content, and *"cost-plus" and "escalator" types of contracts again came to the fore in private industry.
In spite of this condition in civilian construction, the stand was taken by the Minister of Defence Production and the department at the beginning of the defence production program that the work would be carried out on the basis of public competition firm prices contracts; that no escalator proposals would be accepted, and that work would be carried out on a cost plus fixed-fee basis only in those cases where security, military urgency and lack of plans and specifications, or the remoteness of the work, left no alternative.
Thus, at a time when a large volume of civilian construction was being carried out on a cost-plus basis the defence construction program, with the basic exception of projects of a strict security nature, was on a firm price competitive basis. You will appreciate that this placed contractors operating on firm prices for defence construction in an unenviable position in competing for labour and materials against the many large industrial projects being carried out on cost-plus or similar negotiated terms. Immediately come to mind the large industrial projects in Quebec and Ontario, the oil and chemical developments in Alberta, the Kitimat project in British Columbia, all involving hundreds of millions of dollars in construction expenditures.
The Budget-Mr. Dickey
At this point it should be emphasized that in connection with the construction projects of a strict security nature, and a few other instances, there has been no alternative but to let the work on a cost plus fixed-fee basis. The terms of these contracts in regard to cost control are much stricter than those normal in private industry. Fees are not the contractors' profit. Head office expenses for managerial, engineering and purchasing personnel are not allowed as an item of cost against the contract, but must be recovered by the contractor from the fee. The fees paid are fixed fees based upon a standard scale. The scale is based upon 5 per cent up to $2 million, reducing to 4 per cent for a project costing between $2 million and $3 million and reducing again to 3 per cent for any excess of the projected cost over $3 million. Since the fee, while based upon a percentage, is converted to a fixed fee on the execution of the contract, no advantage accrues to the contractor from increasing the cost of the work.
In so far as our defence construction program is concerned, the only exceptions are on the following bases:
First, jobs which for normal commercial reasons, or other causes, contain no element of profit; for example, the provision of power facilities and the building of railroad sidings and similar services;
Second, jobs of a strict security, nature. Jobs of this nature cannot be let out to tender, first of all for the normal reasons of security which extend over the entire performance of the contract from the beginning to the completion of the work and, second, because of the inappropriateness of sending out detailed plans and specifications of secret projects to anyone requesting and making the requisite deposit for them.
The third main reason which may dictate variance from the normal procedure of calling tenders can be the urgency of the need of the Department of National Defence for the particular facility required.
The fourth may be the necessity of commencing construction of a project while plans and specifications for later stages of the same project are being developed.
A fifth reason is the impossibility, in certain circumstances, of construction firms being able closely to estimate the cost of doing the work in extremely inaccessible locations, which would have the possible effect of all tenderers including an unjustified element of insurance against unforeseen developments.
I would like now to describe the various classes of contracts which come under the

The Budget-Mr. Dickey general description of cost-plus. The first are the contracts which contain no element of profit, and can be referred to as cost-alone contracts. These are entered into with bodies such as various hydroelectric commissions for the construction of power transmission lines, the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific railways for the construction of necessary sidings and other railway facilities to serve defence installations. These contracts are subject to strict cost control.
The second class of contracts can be termed cost plus fixed-fee contracts. These contracts are subject to strict cost control, including audit, and other controls with which I shall deal in a moment.
For defence construction work there are no cost-plus contracts, in the sense of contracts for which the terms provide payment of the total cost of the work, plus a percentage of that cost. Any suggestion that there are contracts of this nature in our defence construction program must be based upon misrepresentation or ignorance of the facts.

Let me say at once that it is not the practice to engage architects or consultants on a cost-plus basis. The services of architects or consultants are obtained for defence construction-

-in which event Defence Construction Limited engage an architect or an engineer to carry out such design in accordance with the physical requirements of the project as laid down by the Department of National Defence.
When the services of a consultant are required, the first step is to select a man or a firm of the highest standing and best technical qualifications obtainable. The contractual arrangements are the normal type of arrangements in connection with professional work of this kind. These arrangements call for the consulting engineer or architect to be paid a percentage of the cost of the work to be designed. Progress payments are made during the design period, and when the project has been built the consultant is paid the agreed percentage of the actual cost of construction. If for any reason the project does not proceed beyond the design stage the consultant is paid an agreed percentage of the estimated cost of the work, such estimate being the subject of mutual agreement between Defence Construction Limited and the consultant.

If the project has been let as a firm price contract, the fee of the consultant is determined as a percentage of that price. If the project has been let as a cost plus fixed-fee contract, the fee is determined on the actual cost of the contract. All consultant contracts are subject to audit by the cost inspection and audit division, which certifies them by examination of the accounts and vouchers of the consultants, and which also checks to make sure that the cost of the work on which the percentage fee is based is the actual cost to the crown.
I should like to emphasize that these arrangements are of the same kind as those entered into by private enterprise when it engages architects and engineers to design and supervise construction projects. Occasionally certain consultant services are paid for at daily rates if the type of service performed does not lend itself to calculation on a percentage of the cost of construction. Again this is the normal type of arrangement with the architectural and engineering professions, and is typical of similar arrangements with consultants when engaged by private industry. Examples of such services are surveys, general site investigations, or modifications of standard plans to suit site conditions. Again such charges are all subject to audit by the cost inspection and audit division of Defence Construction Limited.
I should like now to give some figures relative to the amount and value of construction work in our defence program, indicating the success that has been achieved in so arranging the defence construction program that an overwhelming majority of the contracts, both in number and value, are fixed-price contracts concluded as the result of a publicly advertised call for tenders. I should say immediately that we have embarked on a very important and highly secret program of construction jointly with the United States. We are bound by international undertakings to maintain the strictest possible secrecy in connection with this program. It is the program that was dealt with in the exchange of notes tabled in the house by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) on the 25th day of February, 1952, at page 2381 of Hansard.
Because of security restrictions it will not be possible for me to include in the summary I propose to give any of the costs of projects undertaken in connection with this program. The reasons for this were fully stated in the house by the Minister of National Defence on the 29th day of January at pages 1430 and 1431 of Hansard. I might also say that in connection with this program work is being carried out by some of the most
The Budget-Mr. Dickey respected and reliable firms in the Canadian construction industry, and any criticism that is levelled in a general way at this program must naturally be regarded as criticism of these excellent firms who are doing, I believe, a public service.
The figures I wish to put before the house now are as follows. During the period November 22, 1950 to December 31, 1952, Defence Construction Limited awarded 871 construction contracts having a total value of $255,826,000. Both these figures exclude contracts in connection with the program referred to above as excluded by security. Of the 871 contracts 16, with a value of $17,700,000, were contracts coming under the general classification of cost plus fixed-fee contracts. In terms of percentages the 16 cost plus fixed-fee contracts amount to 1-9 per cent of the total contracts awarded and their value to 6 [DOT] 9 per cent of the total value of contracts awarded.
The small percentage deviation from the general policy appears to me to be a significant achievement when one considers the many difficulties which are inherent in construction for defence, almost all of which make it a special problem to follow normal procedures of inviting tenders. Of the considerations I dealt with earlier which dictate the letting of contracts without a public tender call, security is by far the most important. Next in importance is location, which is shown by the fact that the majority of our cost plus fixed-fee contracts are at places such as Goose Bay, Churchill and other similar Arctic or sub-Arctic areas.
Now, Mr. Speaker, admitting the impossibility of completely avoiding cost plus fixed-fee construction contracts in a program of this kind, I should like to deal as completely as I can, but at the same time briefly, with the control procedures which are employed to ensure that these cost plus fixed-fee contracts and other cost contracts are performed in an economical and efficient manner with the maximum elimination of waste or extravagance of any kind whatsoever. This -control is of course a very important part of the responsibility of Defence Construction Limited and the other agencies which are responsible to the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) for the operations under this program. The public servants- who staff these agencies are, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, thoroughly imbued with the necessity for exercising the strictest possible control over every phase of construction operations, whether under cost plus fixed-fee arrangements or not. These control procedures in their entirety apply to all cost plus fixed-fee
2652	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Dickey contracts administered by Defence Construction Limited, including all the projects of a strict security nature to which earlier reference has been made.
Before dealing in detail with the various stages at which effective cost control is exercised, I want to refer to page 2566 of Hansard of Tuesday, March 3, and following pages where the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) stated in this debate that he had oral complaints and letters from individuals disclosing what he termed "waste and extravagance" and "a flagrant disregard of cost" in connection with secret projects. He said he was thereby bringing these matters to the official attention of the government. I invite the hon. member to make available either here in the house or privately to the minister, or to the R.C.M.P. or such other responsible authorities as he may choose, any information he may have in his possession that would permit an immediate and full investigation of the alleged incidents to which he refers. This invitation of course applies generally to all hon. members. All we ask is co-operation in enabling us to get to the bottom of any charges or allegations of this kind in order to eliminate anything in the nature of waste or extravagance, whatever its cause or origin may be.
I recognize that in matters of this kind standards of conscience and views as to what is in the public interest differ, but in my view I do not feel that anyone in this house or outside of it has fully discharged his public duty until he has made available to an appropriate authority any information in his possession which would permit or facilitate the full investigation of any matter where misuse or waste of public funds is suspected.
Turning now to the detail of controls over expenditures on cost plus fixed-fee contracts, Defence Construction Limited first enters the picture in the selection of a consulting engineer for designing and engineering the project if such services are required. Here every precaution is taken to ensure that only firms or individuals of recognized integrity, experience and ability are chosen. Care is taken to see that design and planning are carried out with careful observance of the standards of construction and accommodation laid down in the standards adopted by the Department of National Defence and approved by treasury board.
After the design phase is completed, the utmost care is taken in the selection of a contractor. In this type of contract it is generally agreed that the type of contractor selected is of even greater importance than is the case in a firm price contract. The available firms are all considered with a view [Mr. Dickey. 1

to selecting only contractors of wide experience in the particular type or class of work to be performed. We are carefuil to ensure that the firm or firms to be selected have fully qualified personnel, and that the equipment which they have available for the project is of the proper type and in first-class condition.
The actual contract entered into is itself carefully designed to protect the crown to the fullest possible degree. I have not time to summarize the contract provisions in any detail, but there are several important features to which I should draw attention. The first is that the prime contractor is required to call competitive tenders for all major items of supply of materials or subcontracts. Second, wherever possible the award of subcontracts or supply contracts is on a firm price basis. Third, these awards are only made with the consent of the supervising authority, that is Defence Construction Limited or Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Fourth, salaries payable to the contractor's employees such as engineers, superintendents, draftsmen and foremen shall only be such as shall be approved by the minister. Finally, the entire work in every particular is subject to the control and supervision of the engineer in charge representing Defence Construction Limited who is the sole judge of work and materials and has full power to reject in whole or in part any work which is improper, defective, or insufficiently executed or performed by the contractor. There is, of course, a right under the contract for the work to be taken out of the contractor's hands if it is improperly or unsatisfactorily performed.
An important factor in dealing with contracts of this nature is the definition of items to be included in the cost of the work. This is very carefully and fully provided in the contract by means of a standard schedule which forms part of an agreement between Her Majesty and the contractor. It carefully delineates all items which can be included in the cost of the work; and is, so far as we can possibly ensure, as complete and sufficient as it can be to protect the interests of the public treasury.
Perhaps the most important single item in this whole question of control of costs is the question of careful, efficient and continuous supervision. On projects where a consultant has been employed in connection with design and planning, it has proven most satisfactory to engage the consultant to provide a fully qualified engineer with adequate inspection staff to carry out supervision on the site. This arrangement permits the closest possible

liaison with the design office, facilitating the interpretation of drawings and eliminating unfamiliarity with the type and quality of materials required. It is the duty of the supervising staff to inspect all materials and carefully oversee all workmanship, not only as regards quality but as regards efficiency of performance, to ensure that costs are controlled.
The supervision does not end with the consultant engineer's staff on the work, or other on-site supervision that may be provided. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation acts as agent for Defence Construction Limited, and Central Mortgage and Housing is fully responsible to Defence Construction Limited for the thorough and economical performance of the work. Both the contractor and the consultant or other on-site supervision report to them. In most cases Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have an engineer permanently on the site, and in every case the regional office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation keeps in close touch with the work by means of periodic visits by their regional construction engineer or his staff.
As a further precaution to guard against waste or inefficiency in carrying out the work, the cost inspection and audit division of Defence Construction Limited maintains a representative on the site. It is his duty to check independently on the receipt of all materials for the work; to check all invoices; and to check all payrolls. These receipts, invoices and payrolls are thus cross-checked by the supervisory engineer on the job, by the cost, inspection and audit division representative, and then they are further scrutinized by the Central Mortgage and Housing regional office before they are finally passed to treasury for payment. Even at this final stage they receive a very thorough examination. The treasury officer is required to keep a close check on the work at all times to ensure that the various controls set up at all intermediate stages have eliminated extravagance or improper use of public funds in so far as it is possible to do so.
As a final and over-all check on our whole construction operation I might well point out that Defence Construction Limited, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and the Department of Defence Production have another department of government-the Department of National Defence-actively and intimately following every stage of the work being performed. It is the Department of National Defence that comes to parliament for the money with which these construction bills are paid, and they, when the work is
The Budget-Mr. Dickey completed, accept the finished building or other project for occupation and use. It is obviously a matter of great concern to them that the money they provide to us for the performance of these services is properly and carefully spent, and that the finished product that they must use in their operations for many years to come is in accordance with specifications and suitable for the very important work they must do. They are naturally most exacting in their requirements of us at every stage, and we are very pleased to have this careful and thoroughly independent and final check on the work we are doing. It is from the point of view of the public good an over-all and most effective check on all our operations, both cost plus fixed-fee and otherwise.
From this summary several points stand out with crystal clarity. First the basic policy in the letting of construction contracts has been that economy is best guaranteed through public competitive firm price tenders. The Canadian construction industry, represented by some of its most reputable and efficient operators, is performing this entire program under both firm price and cost contracts. General allegations of waste and inefficiency unsupported by facts are a reflection not only on public servants but also on a number of loyal Canadians who are just as interested as anyone else in efficiency and economy in the expenditure of public moneys.
As a matter of fact, the achievement and performance of the contractors who are working on defence construction projects and the Canadian construction industry generally have been of the highest order. The quality of the construction is good. The progress of the work is also good, particularly when one takes into consideration the magnitude of the program so quickly launched, the problems of planning, shortages of materials and manpower, and the inevitable difficulty of pyramiding such a large program on a construction industry already struggling with the greatest volume of work in its history. Cost-wise the program has been carried out with the greatest of care. There is no better criterion of true cost than the public competitive tender and this has been the keystone of the program, fully effective in over 98 per cent of the contracts and in over 93 per cent of the value of the work.
In those exceptional cases where it has been necessary to resort to a cost type of contract, every effort has been made to select consulting engineers and architects of the highest calibre, to negotiate the construction work with general contractors of acknowledged capacity and integrity and recognized
2654	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Dickey as outstanding in their particular fields. The checks and controls which I have outlined on all expenditures for materials, labour and subcontracts, which are maintained throughout by engineering supervisors on the work and the cost inspection and audit division, leave no doubt that every precaution is taken in the public interest. The defence construction program has benefited from the assistance of the engineering and architectural professions and from the support of the manufacturers, suppliers and contractors engaged on the program, who have shown every desire to carry out the program with economy and efficiency.
It is a tribute to those who have participated in the program that it is now over 70 per cent complete, that the quality of the work continues to improve and the rate of takeover of the completed buildings continues to accelerate from month to month. The record is clear, and calls for no apology.
I must apologize, however, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for having dealt in the main with matters not directly connected with his most admirable and constructive budget. However, I trust that he will agree with me that when wild and general charges are made, completely-I use that word "completely" advisedly-unsupported by facts, such charges requires a prompt and adequate reply in this house.

speechtext: I wonder if the parliamentary assistant would permit a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
