Mr. Speaker, there has been no change in government policy. I judge from what I heard of what the hon. member quoted that he was referring to a design of supervisory contract. In so far as construction is concerned, outside of the strict security program to which I referred there are 16 cost plus fixed-fee contracts and that is all. If 

the hon. member wants any further information the defence expenditure committee expects to get to this very important subject of construction on Tuesday, and the witnesses who will appear before that committee will be delighted to deal with any questions he may have.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am
glad, Mr. Speaker, to be able to follow the speaker who has just resumed his seat because his speech has reflected great credit upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). During world war II the minister conducted the affairs of his department in such a way as to merit, I believe, the honour of Canadians for many generations to come. I am glad the Minister of Trade and Commerce is in his seat and was able to hear the speech.
It is my purpose to discuss today another aspect of the Canadian beet sugar industry. That aspect is Cuba and the Canadian beet sugar industry between two world wars. More specifically I propose to deal with salt fish and potatoes in the maritimes, cane sugar in Cuba and the Bennett administration's 1932 minimum price of $2.30 on sugar in the country of origin for purposes of tariff, which was aimed at protecting the beet sugar industry in Canada. I propose to mention how unscrupulous Liberal politicians played politics with them all. My main purpose in this talk will be to seek to determine whether, and to what extent, maritime sales of salt fish and edible potatoes to Cuba depend upon Canadian purchases of sugar from Cuba.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, there is abroad in the land a very serious amount of misconception and prejudice in respect of this important matter. My speech today, like the three speeches I have already given this session, is designed to put the facts before the people of Canada to enable them to judge for themselves the position of the beet sugar industry. Once people know the facts, they can draw their own conclusions.
May I say a word about the story of Cuba's recent sugar experiences. Cuba was hard hit by a depression, just as all other American countries were. Cuba's sales to the United States in the years 1926 to 1929 averaged 3,543,000 tons a year. Under the Hawley-Smoot tariff this dropped to 1,948,000 tons during 1931 to 1933. Now, that fact alone has played a tremendously important part in the maritime provinces and has been utterly disregarded by the reckless speakers who have gone babbling all over this country telling falsehoods and giving false impressions. Partly because of this tremendous falling off in Cuba's sales, Cuba's purchases of maritime salt fish and potatoes fell off greatly, as you would naturally expect.

I should like to say a word or two as to how the Liberal party made political capital of that situation. Before long certain politicians were circulating stories that the mari-times had lost their Cuban market for dried salt fish because of the $2.30 minimum price on sugar imposed in 1932 by the Bennett administration. The many facts bearing upon this whole matter are clearly and scientifically set forth by Ralph P. Bell in a most instructive article in the Halifax Herald of February 8, 1938, pages 7 and 12, under the heading "A reply to Senator William Duff". From this article I draw the major part of the figures I use in this talk. Mr. Bell is exceptionally well informed in respect of all matters pertaining to sugar, and pretty well all matters pertaining to the maritimes.
The reason for the article is pointed out in an editorial in the same issue of the Halifax Herald entitled "The Public Demand". From this editorial I quote:
On Thursday last Ralph P. Bell, Halifax businessman and a director of the Acadia Sugar Refining Company, delivered an address before the board of trade at Lunenburg. On that occasion Mr. Bell-
1.	Argued in justification of the retail price of sugar to consumers in Canada; and
2.	Declared certain West Indian markets for Nova Scotia fish were not adversely affected as a result of the Canadian sugar duties.
Promptly Mr. Bell's statements were challenged by Hon. William Duff, who held in reply that Canadian consumers of sugar were being exploited behind tariff walls, and that maritime markets for products such as fish and potatoes in the southern countries of Cuba and the Dominican Republic had been all but destroyed as a result of the sugar duties situation. Moreover, Senator Duff asserted, Mr. Bell as a director of a sugar refining company, was not entirely unprejudiced in the discussion.
Today Mr. Bell makes his rejoinder which appears in full in these columns . . .
From this editorial one can easily gather the fact that the Liberals did attack the $2.30 minimum, and the nature of that attack. They pointed out, for example, that the maritimes had sold Cuba dried salt fish to the value of 101,000 quintals in 1925, and only
46,000	quintals in 1936. They blamed this loss upon Canada's imposition on January 30, 1932 of the $2.30 minimum price on Cuban raw cane sugar in Cuba. The figures had a spectacular look, especially to people uninformed as to the facts and unable to gain access to them.
These politicians omitted to give their hearers and readers two other important facts. These figures revealed that the maritimes sold Cuba 67,000 quintals in 1930 and 21,600 quintals in 1932, the last two years before the imposition of the $2.30 minimum. If these politicians had given all four of those 68108-169
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore figures, the full set would have looked like this:
Tear	Quintals
1925	  101,000
1930	  67,000
1932	  21,600
1936	  46,000
These figures would have spoiled the fun entirely for the Liberal politicians. These figures show, first, that maritime sales of salt fish to Cuba fell off 34 per cent from 1925 to 1930; second, that such sales of salt fish by the maritimes to Cuba fell off by at least a very considerable part of 45,400 quintals or over 67 per cent between 1930 and 1932, before the $2.30 imposition; that for the four years after 1932, after the application of the $2.30 per hundredweight valuation for duty purposes in the land of origin, maritime salt fish sales to Cuba increased to 46,000 quintals, an increase of 24,400 quintals or over 100 per cent, after the so-called dumping duty which was supposed, in their words to have ruined entirely the market for salt fish and potatoes for the maritimes. These figures, of course, give the absolute lie to the Liberal propaganda concerning the $2.30 minimum price and resultant loss of maritime salt fish sales to Cuba.
But here is another set of figures more damning still to the Liberal position. Cuban purchases of salt fish from all the world between 1932 and 1936 increased from 110,000 quintals to only 160,000 quintals, an increase of less than 50 per cent. Look at those figures again. For the four-year period, 1932 to 1936, Cuban purchases of salt fish from all the rest of the world increased less than 50 per cent. From Canada Cuban purchases of salt fish during the same period increased over 100 per cent. In other words, in terms of percentages Cuban purchases of salt fish from the maritimes of Canada, who bought no Cuban sugar from 1932 to 1936, grew by practically twice as much as did her purchases of salt fish from the rest of the world which presumably had no $2.30 sugar minimum value in the place of origin, and which therefore presumably bought Cuban sugar during that period.
The conclusion to be drawn from these facts must be that Cuban purchases of maritime salt fish do not depend upon Canadian purchases of sugar from Cuba.
Mr. Speaker, it is of the utmost importance that the maritime people and the Canadian people get this fact firmly fixed in mind today. Otherwise terrible mistakes can be made during the next few years. Incidentally, I will stop to say that the fact that these stories have been circulating indicates the

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore industry. And countless Liberals did that very thing all across Canada.
Let the maritimes henceforth be warned; let all Canadians be warned and alerted, that they might be wise to be suspicious of every story the Liberals tell them about Cuba and sugar and maritime salt fish and potato markets.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a small potato.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are a lot smaller potatoes that the Liberals have been scattering around all over. They are so small that you can hardly see them without a magnifying glass.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will get you one.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The big lie.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a scandalous, downright shame. I daresay the hon. member has been telling some of these things out in his province of Saskatchewan.
I have said what I desire to say in respect of the beet sugar industry, Mr. Speaker. One of the great things, as I indicated in my opening remarks, is that the rank and file of the people of Canada do not know the facts at all pertaining to the whole question of beet sugar and cane sugar in Canada. They have to rely upon people in public life to learn 'the truth and to tell them the truth. If they do not receive the truth from men in responsible positions, how can they tell what to think and what to demand?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tell the truth and shame the devil.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My whole object in speaking on this subject this afternoon was, as I said, not to be political but to impress upon the people of Canada and upon the members of this house, if I might, that the amount of salt fish and edible potatoes which the maritimes were able to sell to Cuba did not in any way depend upon importations of Cuban sugar into the maritimes, or at least it did not do so in 1938.
I should like to say a word here in respect of the maritimes. I have a very deep sympathy for the maritime provinces. I have given their problems considerable thought now for something like 15 years. There is a problem in the maritimes which must be solved. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) made a speech the other day which I thought very beautiful and very pathetic. Too few people seem to realize that what the hon. member was telling was the truth. The maritime provinces, since they joined confederation, have been bled white. They have had their industries destroyed and


removed. They have had their financial independence destroyed because the headquarters of their banks have been removed to the central provinces. They have had evils inflicted upon them which I confess, Mr. Speaker, are a disgrace to the governments and to the members of the house which permitted these evils to be inflicted.
As the hon. member said the other night in his speech, he hopes he will be able to continue to live in the maritimes; but he is not sure. No wonder he is not sure, when we consider what has been happening in the maritime provinces even since the close of world war II. Something simply must be done with respect to the maritimes if we intend that splendid area to be the great and valuable asset to Canada it is capable of being, not only in the matter of industry but also in that of wealth, of population, of influence and in every other way.
So long as we allow it to continue as it is today, it will be a reflection upon us, and it will be a source of unhappiness to the people who live there. Instead of being a glorious asset it will become more and more a liability, despite the fact that Newfoundland is involved in the maritimes today.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It will be understood that I am not reflecting upon Newfoundland.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not "the maritimes".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is counted as one of the maritime provinces today, is it not?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are not maritimers.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All right. Newfoundland has been enjoying its improved condition for a little while because it has just come into the confederation. But let Newfoundland go on for a few years, until they realize the full impact of policies adopted in Ottawa by all the governments which have sat here since confederation, and Newfoundland will have a very sad story to tell, too.
The first thing the maritime provinces ought to do is have a beet sugar factory of their own. I know there are two splendid cane sugar refineries in the maritime provinces, and I do not wish any ill toward the cane refineries. But when one considers the value of the beet sugar industry to an area such as Alberta, and realizes its value as an asset to that province, he must grant that one of the finest things that could happen to the maritime provinces would be the establishment of a beet sugar industry there which would enable them to supply all their needs, ultimately permitting the cane sugar

refineries to slip out of existence, even if the people who hold those factories have to be bought out.
From this point on today I am speaking entirely as a member of this parliament, just an ordinary Canadian; I am not speaking for the Social Credit group at all. I am simply putting on record some of the ideas I have had when I have been contemplating the problems of the maritimes, ideas that I humbly submit as being possibly worthy of some consideration.
I believe the time has to come when we shall recognize the four maritime provinces- that is, the three of them, and Newfoundland -as an economic zone. They have to have industries in that area. I believe every hon. member in the house would say he believes in the decentralization of industry. What in the world is the use of decentralizing industry if you deny industry the market it ought to have by permitting powerful concerns from Ontario and Quebec to go down into that area and sell goods in competition with goods being produced there, and operate to an extent that the industry there cannot pay?
That is the situation which faces the maritime provinces. What are we going to do about it? As I suggested, we shall have to give those people permission to have an economic zone of their own. It looks to me as though that is the only way in the world in which we shall have any decentralization of industry, a development of the resources of that area, and a retention of its purchasing power, as well as an increase in its population which, of course, would mean a greater market for the goods produced by their industries.
How would this be worked out? It looks to me as though the four maritime provinces would be wise to consult with each other and formulate an agreement to work together. In such a way they would be more valuable to Canada than they can be separately. Let them meet together and work together, to see if they cannot get agreement from the big concerns in Ontario and Quebec-a gentlemen's agreement, if you like-that those concerns will not send their goods into the maritime provinces, beyond a certain point, unless the maritimes request specifically that those goods be sent there. In this instance a quota would be established voluntarily, by the industries in Ontario and Quebec, realizing that as they sell their goods in the maritimes they will require the proper atmosphere and circumstances for the establishment of industries there. I do not see why that sort of thing should not be done. I do not see why under the protection
The Budget-Mr. Gardiner of such an arrangement the maritimes should not build a powerful industrial unit, with high purchasing power, greatly strengthening themselves in every way, and thereby being enabled to develop their resources.
There is no use having fine resources if an area is unable to develop them. What good would the irrigated area of southern Alberta be if we could not establish the industries with which to use the resources of that area? Give the country conditions under which industries can be established, and then you will have in respect of any area an accumulation of population and an increase in purchasing power. You will have industrial strength; you will have a real asset to the Dominion of Canada, as well as a source of taxation and every other thing we desire.
I have made these few comments with respect to the maritime provinces because, after having studied the matter, I am firmly convinced that we never will solve the problem of the maritimes until we do what I have suggested.
I shall have more to say at a later time in respect of the Canadian beet sugar industry, but for the time being I shall make no further comments about the maritimes. There are other facts concerning the Canadian beet sugar industry as it is affected by Cuba, and in connection with policies prepared in Ottawa, which simply must be made clear to the people of Canada. With the permission of the house I am going to endeavour to set out some of those important facts at some future time in this chamber.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on
the budget has now been going on for some considerable time. I was told by one of the members just a few moments ago that I am the fiftieth to address the house. That is, of course, a fairly high number; but since there are something more than two hundred left I presume the number of speakers could grow.
The amendment moved by the financial critic of the opposition deals with a number of matters, but there is only one part of it I am going to discuss at this time. The part with which I am concerned reads:
That all the words alter "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that under the present budget the government proposes to take more money from the taxpayers of Canada than ever before for non-defence and defence expenditures without any effective steps being taken to:"
And then, under that:
-offer any encouragement to Canadian farmers in meeting the serious consequences of lost markets and lower prices resulting from the government's agricultural and marketing policies.
2660	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Gardiner
It is that part of the amendment to which I wish to address myself in the time at my disposal. I should like first to state to members of the house that a delegation from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, with representatives from right across Canada, met with us today, and they have left with us a memorandum covering the views of the federation with regard to agricultural policy and the condition of farmers in general throughout the country. I am not going to read that document to the house. I am quite certain that hon. members will be quoting from it from time to time. I am going to suggest, however, that if one reads it carefully, in spite of the fact that there are criticisms of the government, criticisms of the Department of Agriculture and criticisms of general policy, generally speaking the document indicates that those who represent the farmers across this country are fairly well satisfied with the general policy.
They think the floor price on eggs ought to be higher. They think the floor price on hogs ought to be higher. They think the floor prices on some other commodities might be changed to advantage, and that we might have a floor price on poultry products; but they do not suggest that we should change the policy of placing floor prices under farm products as established under the legislation of 1944. In other words they ask us to carry on under the policy which was established in 1944 and to do that, if possible, in a manner which will give a little more support to farmers. But they are not critical of the line of policy, and are not critical of what the government has been doing in general. As a matter of fact, in many sections of their submission to the government they are quite complimentary.
I only say that at this time in order to indicate that the feeling in every part of Canada is not quite the same as it is in the small section of this house represented by the opposition. It may be that there is a group of people in Canada, bearing a comparison reasonably proportionately to those who represent the opposition in the house, who have a feeling somewhat similar to that which has been expressed since the beginning of the budget debate, but I can assure hon. members opposite that view is not held as strongly as they might think, judging from what they have had to say.
For example, it is suggested that we have great quantities of farm products in this country for which farmers are searching for a market. We have some farm products for which a market is being sought, but their proportion compared with the proportion for which farmers have searched for markets in the past is comparatively small. As a matter


of fact we have two surpluses of farm products in Canada at present. One is canned pork products. We canned 98 million pounds of pork as a result of the epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease. We have sold 22 million pounds and we have a balance on hand of 76 million pounds.
That might be considered a surplus of one farm product in a certain form, but I am sure all members realize that we will eventually be able to dispose of that product, largely in Canada. We probably will not find a market for very much of it outside Canada. We will be able to dispose of that product in due course. It is in surplus as a canned product 'largely because of the fact that we took it off the market and put it into a form where it could be preserved and stored for some months and sold finally in markets which we hope will exist for it.
The other product of which we have a surplus on hand for the present is New Zealand beef. We made an arrangement, again associated with the fight that was waged against foot-and-mouth disease, for an exchange of New Zealand beef for Canadian beef in the British market. The New Zealand beef was shipped to the United States and is being sold there. The amount shipped to the United States was 59 million pounds. The amount sold was 48 million pounds and the balance left is something over 11 million pounds. That amount will be sold in due course and will thus be taken off the market. These are the two commodities of which there is a surplus, that we may be said to have some little difficulty in marketing, and that we may have some difficulty in marketing in the months that lie ahead. But apart from that, there is no troublesome surplus of farm products to be found at present.
It is true that we have considerable wheat in Canada, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has reported to us from time to time that the main difficulty ' in connection with the marketing of wheat is to find ways and means of shipping it. It is not a question of finding a market for it. The problem is one of finding shipping facilities to take the wheat from where it is to where it is required. That again is something which gives employment to a great many people in the country and is not a matter of such great difficulty as might be indicated by the speeches we have heard in the house.
I want first to emphasize the fact that we are not in a position where we are worried greatly at present because of the fact that any markets have been lost. As a matter of fact I have some doubt whether "lost" is the

word to use with respect to our markets. We have not lost markets if we are able to market the greater part of our products that are in surplus in a natural way and without any great difficulty. If any market has disappeared for the time being, we have found other markets to take those products, and our farm products are being marketed at higher prices.
The suggestion has been made in discussing the question that it may be because production has been reduced that we are able, to market our farm products. In order to correct any statement of that kind that might be made, or any idea that might prevail to that effect, I am going to place on Hansard figures from a table having to do with production during the last six years compared with the six years preceding the war.
Some may say well, why not take the war years? I do not think it would be fair to the house, to farmers or to anyone to take the war years. Conditions during wartime are always particular conditions that require particular treatment.
Taking the last six years before the war and the last six years we have just gone through, I want to give these figures by way of comparison between the two periods. I am only going to deal with the five products upon which agriculture generally depends for its prosperity-wheat, hogs, cattle, milk and eggs.
During the six years since the war we have produced on an average 162 million bushels of wheat more per annum than in the six years before the war, which is approximately one-half more. During the six years since the war we have produced on an average 360 million pounds more pork per annum than in the six years before the war, which is approximately one-half more. During the six years since the war we have produced 270 million pounds more beef per annum than in the six years before the war, which is about one-third more. During the six years since the war we have produced 1,600 million pounds more milk per annum than in the six years before the war, which is one-ninth more. During the six years since the war we have produced 110 million dozen more eggs per annum than in the six years before the war, which is 50 per cent more.
Now, I only need to repeat these figures, and if I were to add some of the other products it would be more apparent that agriculture in this country has annually been producing more and more in the way of food products, since the war, than she ever produced before. As a matter of fact, if one were to make comparisons between the years
The Budget-Mr. Gardiner after the war and the years during the war, one would find that we were producing grain from much less acreage during the war than we are now; but if we weighed up the tonnage of food of one kind and another being produced in this country now we would find that it is much greater than it has been at any other time in our history.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But what about prices?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am going to deal with
them right away, so don't get in a hurry, because you might be disappointed. Prices on these five products will average at least 65 per cent higher, but the difference is best represented in the gross farm income of the last six-year period compared with the preceding period. The average annual total for the last six years was $2,700 million and for the previous period $780 million, or about four times as much.
Well, that is not a bad situation to be confronted with at present. I quite agree with those who represent farm organizations and who represent rural seats in this house, that it is not as good a condition as we farmers would like to have.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are always hopeful of
having better conditions in the future than we have had in the past; but I am sure that farmers in general are satisfied with this statement as a true statement regarding their position: that their position has been improving rapidly from 1945 when the war ended down to 1951; that there was no falling back over the period either in connection with production or in the matter of prices received.
When markets disappeared for one particular product the farmer readily switched over to the production of something else for which there was a ready market. He therefore has been able to market his products over recent years at a very high return.
Coming to that one year, 1951, I wish to point out that it is the highest price year we have ever experienced in agriculture in this country. I think I might say that 1951 produced the highest price levels that have ever been experienced in the history of farming in the United States. So when we make a comparison with 1951-whether we go before that date or whether we follow after that date into 1952 and 1953-it is true that you can show that farm prices were lower in the years prior to 1951. You can also show that farm prices are lower in 1952 and 1953 than they were in 1951; but there is no other year or any other period of years prior to 1951 when you can show higher
2862	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Gardiner price levels or higher production on our farms than can be shown for 1952 and 1953 up to date.
I am only going to call your attention to one matter which is in this report I referred to a few moments ago. They make reference here to a statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech, and they say:
The seriousness of the downward trend from 1951 was clearly indicated by the Hon. Mr. Abbott, Minister of Finance, in the presentation of his recent budget, when he reported a preliminary figure for net farm income for 1952 to be $1,861,000, a decrease of 12 per cent from 1951.
Again I repeat that is the only year you can take to make a comparison and say that 1952 may be lower when the final figures are out in connection with returns for last year. A much sounder kind of (Comparison to make is that which is referred to in the last paragraph on this page. The federation says this:
We wish to maintain and improve these features of our present program which have given agriculture some desirable measure of stability . . .
Referring to government policy-
. . . but at the same time we wish to explore and evolve a more complete and co-ordinated national policy for agriculture with longer term security than can be provided under present day programs.
My comment with regard to that, Mr. Speaker, is that in the first paragraph which I read, the findings of the document are based upon a one-year comparison. I suggest that if they take a three-year comparison or a two-year comparison or a four-year comparison, there is no possibility of coming to the same conclusion that they can come to by comparing 1952 with 1951. The year 1951 is the exceptional year.
It is exceptional in another way, Mr. Speaker. I have been examining figures in order to find out just where we stand in connection with the criticisms which are being made in this house and outside. I find it to be a very remarkable thing that the farm implement companies did not change their prices in 1951. I find that the farm implement companies did change their prices in the years preceding 1951 and they changed their prices in the year following 1951. On some of the most important farm implements used on farms in Canada they lowered the prices in 1952 as compared with 1950. On others they increased prices. On one of the important farm implements the price was increased the day after Christmas in 1952, which is not very long ago.
I am going to suggest to you that if we examine the records very carefully we do not find that the situation has been created in just the way some suggest. My mind
fMr. Gardiner.]

goes back to the time when I entered this house first and we demanded that we have a committee of this house set up to examine into the cost and distribution of farm implements. Out of that investigation came the fact that farmers have invested in farm implements, or to put it another way that the farmer's cost of operation is represented by farm implements to the extent of from 3 to 6 per cent annually.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What year was that?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was in 1936 or 1937.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There has been a big change since then.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Don't get in a hurry; I am
going to tell you what it is right now. I had an examination made today into the figures; and while they are higher, a>s my hon. friend says, than they were back at that time still they are only from 8 to 9 per cent. When you take the total cost of operations on the farms across Canada at present, the proportion of that cost which is capable of being properly checked off to farm implements is from 8 to 9 per cent. It is quite a bit, but it is not sufficient to permit members to stand up in this house and leave the impression that all the increased cost in connection with farm operations is due to something that has happened in connection with farm implements. I think we ought to give all the facts. We ought to consider the facts, and we ought to base our decision upon the facts, whatever they are. I am giving them, Mr. Speaker, for what they are worth.
There is another matter that I wanted to take up which relates to this same question. Over and over again it has been said that the policy of the government in connection with prices and in connection with encouraging production is pretty well based upon the Agricultural Prices Support Act of 1944. We have been making comparisons between what that act takes as the basis of its operations, and the position from time to time. In order to do that it is necessary to take not one year but three years. I am, therefore, going to take the three years upon which we based our provisions for support, and then take the last three years for which we have records. This includes 1951 which, as I indicated a moment ago, was the year in which we had the highest prices.
Let us take cheese, which is the first item in the group of commodities I have here. In 1943-45 we had a price of $1.91 per hundredweight at the farm for cheese. The average actual volume of production was 20 million hundredweight and the average annual farm value-I am just going to use the round figures-was $38 million. In

1949-51 the price was $2.46 per hundredweight, the average annual volume of production 11,600,000 hundredweight, and the average annual farm value $28,700,000. You will note that the total return for cheese was less in the last three years than it was in the three years at the end of the war. That is the only commodity on the list I have of which that can be truthfully said, and that list runs right down the page.
Let us take the next one, butterfat. In 1943-45 the average return for butterfat per year was $187 million, and $237 million in 1949-51. Then for hogs: 1943-45, the average farm price was $16.84 per dressed hundredweight, and in 1949-51 the price was $30.11.

In so far as cattle are concerned, that statement is even more applicable. The average annual farm value for the first three-year period was $187 million, and $385 million for the last three-year period. For apples it was $18 million and $20 million; that is one product of which we have had more delivered and have not received very much more for them. We had more apples delivered in the last three-year period than in the first three-year period, but we only received $20 million for them as against $18 million. For eggs the total for the first
The Budget-Mr. Gardiner period is $107 million, and for the last period $136 million; for potatoes, $78 million and $85 million; for wheat, $441 million and $722 million; for oats, $249 million and $317 million; for barley, $131 million and $206 million.
I give those figures in order to emphasize the position I took a few moments ago, namely that there is not a decrease in the quantity of farm products being produced in this country, either in the last three years as compared with the last three years of the war or in the six years since the war as compared with the last six years before the war. Our production is going up, and going up continuously; and while it is going up prices are increasing and therefore the returns to the farmer are increasing from year to year. If we liked to take it over the longer period, as the federation suggests, from the three-year period at the end of the war to the three-year period now, the same picture is presented.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the minister any tables on farm costs that are comparable?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Farm costs are covered by the second table in the fact that there is a comparison between the first three-year period and the second one, and there is an indication there of the relationship of costs to returns.
I should just like to say that that comparison indicates fairly clearly that it is quite fair to take a gross return from farmers right across Canada rather than just to deal with particular products. It indicates that on wheat, cattle and hogs the margin between cost and return is quite wide, but that on some other commodities there is little if any margin between the cost of production and the return which is received.
I think it will be generally agreed by members of the house that on the average farm across, this country, in so far as obtaining returns is concerned, the more important products are cattle, hogs, grain and products of that kind. Products such as eggs, for example, are important to a group of egg producers who are close to cities; and to some of the fluid milk-producing farms, milk may be the important product from their point of view; but when one looks at all the farms of the whole country, I think one will agree that it is important that there be a considerable margin as between the costs and the returns that are received for the staple products, even if some of the products which do not enter largely into gross returns from the farm show on departmental tables little margin between cost and return.
In listening to the speeches which have been delivered over the past few days in connection with the budget, I have been of the opinion that too much consideration was 68108-1704
being given to the idea that our production was down. I have attempted this afternoon to indicate that this is not the case but that our production is up. Then I was concerned about the fact that an attempt was made to show that our returns were down, and I think I was able to demonstrate by these tables, if not by what I said this afternoon, that our returns are also up. The returns being up and the production being up, the farmer is obtaining more for his efforts across the country than at any other time in our history.
The other matter I have been concerned about is the fact that the opposition in general and the official opposition in particular think we have been here too long. I should like to ask them why they think we have been here as long as we have. I have some ideas of my own about it. I remember that many years ago I came to Ottawa to hear a budget speech. It was the first budget speech delivered by the late R. B. Bennett following the election of 1930. He was his own finance minister and delivered his own budget speech. The speech was a typical Conservative one, as was to be expected. We had just had an election. The Liberal party had been in power for some time, and they had been voted out of power. Those of us who came here and who had supported the Liberal policy were a little bit concerned about what we were going to hear and about what we would probably see.
I came here as a farmer from western Canada, dressed as farmers are dressed; and I was a little bit surprised to find that our Conservative friends had gone back to the time of Sir John A. Macdonald even in the matter of dress. They had their canes. Some of them had their silk hats. Practically all

The Budget-Mr. Gardiner of them had their striped trousers and their long-tailed coats. I did not feel at home anywhere else, so I crawled into a seat up behind that post over there in the gallery where you are not able to see the central benches. It was the only seat I could find. The others seemed to be filled by people who wanted to hear the first budget of the Conservative party after they had come into office.
The only way I could see the speaker when he was delivering his budget was to edge around that post up there occasionally, look down here and get a view of him. I want to say that it was a good speech. There are one or two sentences in it that I want to read to you this evening. Here is one of them, delivered by the leader of the Conservative party at that time:
The resolutions that are being submitted to this house are not for the purpose of affording protection in the sense in which that term is usually used: but if that term is used to designate just what we, during the election, indicated that it did mean namely, the giving to Canadians an equality of opportunity with others who are building up their country to enable us to build up our dominion, and to give fair competition to the worker in Canada, be it man or woman, then it is protection that we propose. There can be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, in the mind of any hon. gentleman within sound of my voice that this government at least has a mandate to give effect to that policy. In every part of this dominion I was at great care to make it known to the audiences who listened to what I had to say, so that there could be no mistake as to what I meant, that in the event of their supporting candidates of our party they thereby supported a policy that would ensure fair competition to Canadian workmen and workwomen and equality of opportunity to Canadians to build up their country.
The remainder of the speech is in agreement with that sentiment. That government was in power for five years; and if anyone has any doubt as to why, the Canadian farming population have never forgotten that. I should just like to read a few of the results that were obtained in so far as agriculture was concerned. The export price of wheat during that period averaged 68 cents a bushel; oats averaged 33 cents a bushel, and cattle averaged $61.93 a head. That was not a hundredweight or a pound, although they have been up to about half that per hundredweight recently. It was $61.93 a head. Beef and veal-these are prices at which products that were being exported, not products that were being consumed in Canada-averaged 5 cents a pound; bacon and hams, 14 cents a pound; cheese, 12 cents a pound and so on.
I think that will give the house the best reason that could possibly be found as to why the Canadian people have left us here for 17 years, now going on toward 18 years. It also gives us reason to understand why I think I would be safe in saying more than 60 per

cent of the members who sit on this side of the house were elected as a result of the votes of the rural people in the constituencies which we represent.
That being the case I can quite understand why those who sit on this side of the house are quite ready to accept the challenge of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). Those of us who represent constituencies all across this country are not at all concerned about when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) decides that it is a good time to go to the country. We do know that when my hon. friend goes up to his own constituency he will have his own troubles. He will probably have difficulty in having himself elected, particularly if he speaks the way he spoke during the session preceding this one. Someone suggested the other evening that he had changed his opinions. I think maybe he has.
I doubt very much if he has actually changed the views he holds either with regard to his own business or the methods by which he can make a success of it, but he has probably found it necessary to express some other views in order to appeal to the people he is going to ask to support him.
But in any case, whether the election comes soon or whether it is delayed for some time, I am quite sure that members sitting on this side will feel that they have policies to present to the agricultural population across this country which are acceptable to that population. As I indicated this afternoon, we have had reports to that effect right across the country. When one appears in areas where there is a farm population it is usually quite evident that this government still holds pretty much the same place in their affections that it held when we went to the country the last time. So when we go next time we expect, unless the Conservative party can find a better policy than the one they enunciated in this speech I was reading a few moments ago or, failing that, unless they find themselves in agreement as to what their policy ought to be, they will experience some considerable difficulty in getting support in agricultural areas across the country.
As far as our friends of the C.C.F. are concerned, no doubt we will have some battles with them out in Saskatchewan, and as we have them we will probably enjoy them; but I expect that unless a different attitude is taken toward the establishment and handling and control of farm prices in that area than has been taken until now, our difficulties will not be as great as they have been on some previous occasions. It has been established in the minds of all the people right across Canada that the situation which existed during the ten years of war and the period following the war no longer exists.

This government has no control over the setting of prices of farm commodities within the provinces; the provincial governments have had that control. It is a remarkable thing that the most radical of all governments in Canada has done the least about it while the most conservative of-all governments in Canada, that of Ontario, has done the most about it. That government has set up boards to control the marketing of farm commodities as provided by our constitution, and they have been dealing with the matter.
I would also point out that since we last met the farm organizations of Canada have realized and are now putting forth the contention that the bringing of vegetable oils into this country and converting them into substitutes for dairy products is something to be dealt with by the provinces. I think at the present time seven provinces have legislation before their legislature or are preparing to place it before their legislatures, dealing with that matter.	[DOT]

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of his speech the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) mentioned that he was the fiftieth speaker in this debate. I rather hesitate to come to bat after such a home run king as the minister. I am asking myself whether I can measure up to the task of opening the second half of this game.
It is therefore with a full consciousness of my limitations that I venture to register my disapproval of the 1953 budget as a whole, and my determination to support the amendment thereto so ably presented and moved by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Mac-donnell). My contribution to this debate will not, I hope, prove repetitious, as I will endeavour to limit myself to possible budgetary repercussions on my own constituency.
I have listened with great interest to the masterful expose made by the financial critic of the official opposition. In my submission he has spoken as a philosopher, as a real financier and, most especially, as a true Canadian conscious of the needs of his fellow men, concerned with the profligate and reckless manner in which the present government has been spending the taxpayer's money, and most particularly anxious to proclaim to the Canadian people the government's utter lack of solicitude for the common man, the everyday labourer, the small wage earner, the father of a family.
I have also listened to the leaders of the C.C.F. and Social Credit groups, and I have been impressed by their opposition to this budget, which the Canadian Congress of Labour has very rightly and truly stigmatized as a budget for the greedy, not for the needy.
After the arguments so ably marshalled by these masters, as well as by other opposition speakers, what possible new arguments could a newcomer to this house possibly build up without cribbing from previous speakers? Hence I prefer to let well enough alone, and to confine myself, first, to a reference to some statements made by certain members who rose to speak in defence of the budget and,

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud especially, in laudatory adulation of its creator; and, second, to certain extracts from the budget speech itself which may be of interest to my constituents, with a view to enlarging and commenting thereupon.
In his opening remarks last Wednesday the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage), after referring to an article in the New York Times, had this to say, as reported at page 2388 of Hansard:
If the writer of that article had been sitting in my seat last Thursday evening, he would have seen across the alley nothing but green, pale, grey faces, gloomy with envy and jealousy, and of course with disappointment.
This was my hon. friend's observation from his point of vantage. As could be expected, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) had to parrot this reference in his speech last Friday. What did we see and observe from this side of the house on budget night on the faces of government members? We saw their faces getting longer and longer.

A person supposed to possess magical or supernatural power derived from alliance with the devil, or with evil spirits.

I call myself a wizard as well; but that is only the polite term for conjurer; in fact, I should think that wizard meant an astrologer, and more of a fortune teller.

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud included, at least a quarter of a million dollars a year. Let not my hon. friend be overanxious and overimpatient. The Liberal government had been in office in New Brunswick, like its counterpart at Ottawa, since 1935. It left its successors in a morass of financial difficulties which will necessarily take the businesslike government of Hon. Hugh John Flemming considerably more than five months to clear up and clean up.
Before passing to something more important than the unwarranted utterances of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley), I should like to quote what two of our New Brunswick daily papers have to say about the Flemming government's first budget. The Telegraph-Journal, published in my hon. friend's own city and well known to him, had an editorial,on the 25th of February on the New Brunswick budget which reads in part as follows:
The intended plan of the government as outlined by the budget speech is to proceed along businesslike lines shunning avoidable expenditures but at the same time rejecting any idea of plunging into a strict "austerity program" which might defeat its own purpose by slowing up the progress of New Brunswick's economy ... It was a confident speech, one which reflected much optimism for the future of New Brunswick, and it was noteworthy also for the evident care which was taken to express its reasoning in non-technical terms so that it would be clearly understood by the citizens.
The Moncton Times of the 26th of February calls the Patterson budget "A Build Up New Brunswick Budget" and reads in part as follows:
The first budget of the new Progressive Conservative government, as presented to the legislature this week by Hon. Donald D. Patterson, provincial secretary-treasurer, gives the people of New Brunswick a clear-cut yet comprehensive outline of the financial position of their province. To many, that picture will be a surprise because a sequence of reported annual surpluses over several years had tended to convey the impression of a more sound state of the province's fiscal structure than actually prevailed.
After referring to the aims of the present Flemming government, the editorial concludes as follows:
These three aims and the adoption of a cautious thrifty policy could mean a great deal in bringing a prosperous economy to this province.

Reductions are proposed on two important categories of equipment used in the fishing industry, namely gasoline engines and wire rope. In the case of the mining industry the proposals include reductions on certain specialized equipment.

The minister will permit me to suggest that he could not have intended to restrict these reductions to gasoline engines only, as a reference to tariff item No. 440k, at page 2143 of Hansard, indicates that it undoubtedly includes all type of engines. Under tariff item 403 the duties on wire rope or cable, for use exclusively in commercial fishing, have been reduced from 25 per cent to 10 per cent under the most-favoured-nation tariff, which would include imports from the United States, while imports from the United Kingdom are now duty free. May I observe, however, that this reduction would have been doubly welcomed by the fishermen who must purchase this very expensive steel rope if it had been accompanied by the elimination of the 10 per cent sales tax which they will still be called upon to pay. Then there would have been real, appreciable and substantial benefits accruing from this budget to those fishermen. The dragger type vessel owners are the ones mostly interested in steel rope, while the great bulk of our fishermen use, and use plenty, ordinary rope of hemp or manila fibre. The budget is silent on this most important commodity to the greatest number of our fishermen. There is no reduction whatsoever in existing duties and sales tax levies on ordinary rope. In my submission this is where substantial cuts should have been made.
Under tariff item No. 682, which has been left untouched by the present budget, the only rope which is duty free is rope not exceeding 1J inches in circumference. This same rope, "not exceeding 1J inches in circumference for the fisheries", quoting from schedule III of the Excise Tax Act, is also exempt from the sales tax. But you will realize, Mr. Speaker, that this is indeed a very small rope. It is only a cord about the size of my little finger, roughly half an inch in diameter, almost a clothesline. Our fishermen have little practical use for that very small rope. It is much bigger and stronger rope that they would mostly need and use. Yet all this rope exceeding 1J inches in circumference falls under tariff item 575 and it becomes subject to the following ad valorem duties: Under the British preferential tariff, 20 per cent; under the most favoured nation tariff, 22 per cent, and under the general tariff 25 per cent.
I am informed that there has been no modification in the above rates since 1925. Hence our fishermen are really hard hit by the duty-axe on the rope which they need

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud (Translation) :
A mineral deposit which could be the most promising ever discovered in New Brunswick.
Since the ore comes from an almost solid vein of pyrite, it is natural to believe that there will be required a sulphur or acid development in connection with any smelting process. From the point of view of tonnage, there are indications of high possibilities. If we go by test drillings 200 feet in depth, it is estimated that the production will be 28,813 tons of lead-zinc ore per vertical foot. Down to a depth of 1,000 feet, this would mean a production of 28,813,000 tons. The deepest drill-hole, so far, goes down to 500 feet.
(Text):
I stated that the response to what the Northern Miner of February 12 referred to as "the exciting new Bathurst field" was also generous. Cash has been pouring in for the development of this most promising find since its discovery.
It should be said that this strike did not mushroom overnight. During the last two or three years pioneer prospectors and mining engineers had been working hard and with commendable perseverance in our district. Gloucester county, the province of New Brunswick, and Canada ias a whole owe these pioneers an eternal debt of gratitude.
May I be permitted to make special mention of two of these precursors of our new era of prosperity. First there is our own "Pat" Meahan, a Bathurst-born mining engineer with a great faith in his native county. For several years past he has been exploring our back country. He had confidence in our mining potentialities; he never got discouraged; he kept on "plugging". Truly, the name of Pat Meahan deserves special mention in the mining annals of New Brunswick. Then we have Mr. M. J. Boylen of Toronto, whose courage, perseverance and confidence in our mineral deposits have finally enabled him to reap a richly deserved reward. The editor of the Northern Miner rightly remarked:
With this discovery, Mr. M. J. Boylen is assured a place in the mining hall of fame . . . But now while still a young man he has reached a pinnacle that is attained by few.
Publicly sponsored companies, with over seven millions in their treasuries, are already working on their holdings. This estimate, of course, does not include operating companies such as Mining Corporation, Noranda, Anacon and others, which have already fortified themselves with extensive property holdings in our new base metal field. An important United States group has lately entered our mining picture. Strategic Materials Corporation, headed by an important group of prominent United States industrialists and financiers, are now interested in vast staked holdings. In his first official declaration after


the strike, Hon. Hugh John Flemming, our new premier, was quick to assure all mining interests of the full co-operation of our provincial government.
On the 24th of February our New Brunswick provincial secretary-treasurer, Hon. D. D. Patterson, in his first budget speech, after referring to the various phases of the general economy of our province said:
My main emphasis is to refer to the announcement last month of what is reputed to be a new important mining discovery located in northern New Brunswick, in the Bathurst area. There would seem little doubt that this development may be the spark to usher in a new era for New Brunswick.
As for the federal Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, I am already assured of their co-operation. It is our hope, in Bathurst, that we may soon have the honour of receiving in our midst the minister of that department. I have no doubt that his visit, on the spot, will convince him of our vast mining potentialities and will confirm our confidence in the survey, assaying and other laboratory tests of his department.
May I suggest that it is the hope of my constituents that through his department further aeromagnetic surveys will be conducted in the county of Gloucester. I am informed that it is possible that more ore bodies may be detected should, such a survey be made from the old Bathurst mines through Allardville, Paquetville, St. Isidore to Caraquet and along the shores of the bay of Chaleur including, of course, Shippigan, the Islands, Inkerman and Tracadie.
We would also welcome, and we solicit, the assistance of both the federal and provincial departments of mines to make surveys and assist in the exploration and possible development of the coal deposits which we know to exist at Maltampec, extending as far as the shore of Pokesudi. In other words, Gloucester county has now been proved to be an important base metal territory, and we feel that our governments should spare no effort in assisting in its development to the fullest possible extent.
Likewise may I make an appeal to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). There is at present a 16-mile dilapidated railroad running from the main Canadian National Railways line, at or near Gloucester Junction, to Bathurst Mines. At present it is only used by a motorized trolley car. I understand that work is already proceeding on rehabilitation of this line. This practically abandoned spur line has now become a vitally important link between the new mine field and the town of Bathurst; it should be properly rebuilt at once, and put in shape for the heavy loads that will result when the mines are in production.

A good new highway is also urgently needed to link the mines with Bathurst. We already have the assurance that our provincial government will soon undertake this important construction.
I know that the genial Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) would certainly feel surprised, if not offended, were I to forget his department in my plea for governmental assistance in the wake of the major developments that are in store for Gloucester county as a result of our gigantic mining expansion. I am informed that by the middle of April the size of the mill to be erected in the vicinity of Bathurst will be decided. At present a mill with a minimum capacity of 5,000 tons of ore daily is contemplated, but new discoveries with consequent increased profit potentials could possibly raise this objective. This necessarily predicates harbour facilities for exporting our mining products. Major developments will naturally be needed in the Bathurst harbour. Deep-sea, year-round navigable harbours are available in Gloucester county. May I just mention two which could be easily developed, the Pointe Marcel harbour, in the parish of Caraquet, and the Ship-pigan harbour. I therefore strongly urge the immediate necessity of thorough surveys into the possibilities and adaptability of these two natural harbours.
This is, in short, the present situation on the mining front in Gloucester county. But what rosy horizons are we not justified in envisaging as the result of these discoveries, in the whole economic future of the province of New Brunswick? All our available hydro power resources will have to be developed for the new industries for which we have been long clamouring, and that will henceforth come to our province. At this stage I wish to thank the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), who spoke so highly this afternoon of the maritime provinces. No longer shall our young men have to desert our county and province to seek employment elsewhere.
One newspaper predicts that the town of Bathurst can set its sights on a population of
40,000	within a few years. In the last paragraph of a recent editorial "Une ere de grande prosperite s'annonce au Nouveau Brunswick", Le Droit says:
(Translation):
The province of New Brunswick, generally considered up to now as a poor province, is now entering upon an era of great prosperity. Canadians have greeted this news with much enthusiasm.
(Text):
While I am the first to realize with the French poet that all the future is in God's hands only, l'avenir est a Dieu, yet the prospects of my county and province never looked
The Budget-Mr. Sinnott so bright and promising as they do now. Our people who have valiantly stood adversity and laboured under hard conditions have all that it takes to make full use of the prosperity which the future holds in store for them. Let us hope that our governments will also accept the challenge. The hardy people of Gloucester county may well today borrow these lines from Alfred Lord Tennyson:
We sailed wherever ships could sail,
We founded many a mighty state,
Pray God our greatness may not fail Through craven fears of being great!
