speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether or not I shall be worthy of that ovation, but I shall do the best I can for the constituency I represent. I am sure we were all glad to hear the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Dickey) this afternoon give a full, detailed-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Fairy story.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -explanation of defence construction, cost-plus construction and so on. While he was giving a thorough analysis of what was going on, I noticed that the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Hodgson), the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne), the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robiehaudi), the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton), the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser), the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), were the only Conservative members in the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And there were about six Liberals.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Name the Liberals.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure that will illustrate how much interest they took in what was going on.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You could not name the Liberals.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am about the fifty-third speaker in this debate on the budget. I do not want to be repetitious, so I shall endeavour to confine my remarks to matters which have not been mentioned.
I am sure that the Liberal party, and the people of Canada as a whole, are more than enthused with the recent budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sure they will all give credit to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in bringing down his eighth budget, for having offered his services to the people of Canada for eight years in that capacity. I am sure there is no other finance minister in the world who has the record of Hon. D. C.

The Budget-Mr. Sinnott Abbott. He has been rendering service to Canada for which all Canadians will be thankful for some time to come. His name will stand as that of one of the most able finance ministers Canada has ever had.
I now turn my remarks to a reference to the financial critic of the Conservative party, the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdon-nell). I am sure those who were here that night when he first got to his feet will be more or less at a loss to understand him. The hon. member for Greenwood was without words as far as criticism of the budget was concerned.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He was dumbfounded that the Grits would bring down such a budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He had not spoken about the budget for more than four or five minutes when he turned to the Currie report. It must have been of more interest to him than criticism of the budget.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Horses.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell you some more about that subject later on. I also heard him over the radio. As a result of hearing the questions asked Hon. D. C. Abbott and the way they were answered, and the questions asked the same man who would have liked to fill this portfolio which Hon. D. C. Abbott is at present filling, the only conclusion one can come to is that Canada would have been in a terrible mess if he had had his wish.
He then turned to a remark that was made by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) about Pickering. In other words Pickering was more in his line of criticism than was discussion about the budget. May I say that in the riding of Springfield we have some towns which have just as much trouble getting water as has Pickering. I refer to the little town of Lac du Bonnet. They did not bother the provincial government, and they did not bother the dominion government. They went in and formed their own co-operative, and they are supplying water to the people in the town at a dollar a month. If some of these towns would themselves show a little bit of initiative instead of trying to lean on others, they would get farther ahead.
I am not going to defend the budget. I am going to let the Ottawa Journal, a Conservative paper, defend it. This is what they bad to say:
The change in the corporation tax with respect to small business is this: For the present rate of tax of 20 per cent, on the first $10,000 of taxable income there is substituted the rate of 18 per cent, on the first $20,000 of taxable income. This is a substantial change, should mean much to those small industries which are the backbone of so many communities, and mean much also for the industry which, with great possibilities before it, is just getting under way and needs money for capital extensions.


That is the Conservative paper, backing up just exactly what this government did.
So much reference has been made to horses that I thought possibly it might be a good thing for me to mention them again. I believe the military critic of the official opposition, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), was on a radio forum some time ago; that he was asked this question: "Were horses on the payroll in the first war?" and that his answer was: "I would rather not answer that question."
I think anyone knows that in the first war horses were used to draw heavy artillery. Horses were used for cavalry in the first war. Any man who has anything to do with a municipality knows that thousands of teams are hired, and they are referred to as man and team. It is therefore nothing new to municipal men. But to a man by the name of Mr. Currie who is in Montreal investigating this matter, it might have been new. It also might have been new to newspapermen. But I am sure it was a disgrace to the affairs of Canada that such cartoons as appeared were carried in the papers. They did not add at all to the prestige of the country. I am sure that the money involved in hiring a few horses from the farmers there to do work that tractors could not do did not mean anything more than $75 in all. But the criticism went out over the length and breadth of this country and throughout the United States, and it had a bad influence and constituted a black mark on our military forces.
I am now going to refer for a moment to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees). He speaks in the house on practically every subject that comes before us, and he criticizes practically every measure that is brought forward because we are not doing enough. This time he was complaining that we were spending too much money. I am sure he cannot have his cake and eat it too. If he expects social services, I am sure that money has to be raised somehow to pay for them.
I wish to refer to an article by Mr. John Fisher, who was on the radio the other night. He was referring to press reports. He had been taking a trip down through the United States, and he said that in almost every paper he found reports of Canada that were all to the good, that Canada was making great, progress. But in this country he said he saw only three reports of how Canada was making progress. If our newspapers in this country gave a true picture of how Canada is forging ahead, I am sure it would be far better for everyone concerned.
I will turn now to-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Page 6.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-some of the taxes about which hon. members opposite are complaining. Possibly they would say that the $955 million that was made available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was not a good thing for the country; and they claim that not enough houses are being built. I say that it has been a good thing, but the government has had to fight financial corporations, insurance corporations and banks because the rate of interest has been low.
If they want to have a large number of houses built, I think money should be made available for those projects at 3 or 3i per cent.
Possibly they would not say that the money which has been made available for building hospitals throughout Canada was a bad thing.
I will refer to my remarks on July 15, 1946. At that time-rthat was before this program was in effect-I said that every small community throughout Canada was in dire need of a hospital. The town in which I resided at that time had been trying to get a hospital for 20 years. Now we come to 1953, and we find that the constituency has 2 large hospitals for which $100,000 was made available by the provincial and dominion governments before the people themselves spent a dime. So I am sure that what the government has done in that line has helped considerably. Almost 45,000 hospital beds are available at the present time over and above 1946.
Almost $81 million has been made available for industrial development at interest rates ranging from 4-J to 6 per cent. I am sure everyone knows how industry has progressed in Canada.
I think I should read a few quotations from what the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) said back in 1948. When I think of the hon. member for Greenwood I cannot help but think of these large financial institutions. I believe he used to be president of the national insurance company or some such company, and a director of several other large companies. When you are a director of large financial institutions you are out to get all the interest you can. Here is what he said, and I quote from page 1383 of Hansard for February 19, 1948:
Let us now deal with the question of low interest. Some people seem to think that if you talk about interest you are touching some sacred thing and that you will arouse every person in this country against you. X am not afraid of that. What is interest? What does artificially low interest mean? It is interest which is kept down by artificial means. It gives us easy money. What do you mean by easy money? Just what we say-lots of money, money easy to get, money
The Budget-Mr. Sinnott
easy to spend, encouraging people to borrow whether it is wise for them to borrow or not, so that the money can be spent.
Then in the next column:
The government, by its credit policy, should not be making it easy for these people to go on expanding.
Here is what I said in reply, and I quote from page 1614 of Hansard of February 25, 1948:
I always thought that the hon. gentleman, in his pleading for the poor man was conscientious in his views, but it is easy to see just whom he represents in advocating higher rates of interest.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the policy of the industrial bank was wrong?
Does he say that the loans to corporations and individuals amounting to $13 million was wrong at low rates of interest?
Does he think that the moneys lent to the provincial governments, cities, towns, and school districts, amounting to $78 million was wrong at low interest rates?
Would he say that the $104-9 million lent by the chartered banks for stocks and debentures was not high enough? Would the hon. gentleman say that the current commercial loans of $1,921 million are not drawing enough interest? Would he say that the loans made to thousands of returned veterans to establish their homes or start in business was wrong?
Would he say that the $31,500,000 lent to farmers under the Farm Improvement Loans Act was wrong because it was issued at a low rate of interest?
It is wrong, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, for anyone to advocate high rates of interest when he will not take the risk and responsibility of investing his money himself.
And then I went on to say:
I claim, Mr. Speaker, that high interest is the cancer of civilization, and until a remedy is found to take its place the strong and the wealthy are always bound to swallow the weak.
Are we going to adopt the policy of high interest rates which was advocated at that time by the financial critic of the opposition, who speaks for the whole Conservative party? I should like to read a few quotations from the Monetary Times annual national review, 1953. When I heard the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) say this afternoon that the municipalities were in dire circumstances, I could not help but think of an article I saw in a paper the other day which referred to the millions of dollars of assistance that had been granted to them by the provinces, and the provinces got a large share of that money from the dominion government. My speech of December 2 refers to what has happened in the province of Ontario, and that province got from the dominion government $123,327,363. That should go a long way toward helping these poor municipalities. Hon. Leslie M. Frost, Q.C., premier of Ontario, states as follows:
New investment in manufacturing is estimated at $507-5 million for this year;

The Budget-Mr. Sinnott That was referring to 1952. He said:
In the national picture, gauged to the high proportions in every province based particularly on their individual economies, Ontario continues as the industrial heartland, the chief fabricator for the nation. This and other factors have in turn reflected to the benefit of our people, resulting in better and improved living, in obtaining the finest and most from life, in building toward sound economy and the best and most prudent means of using our God-given natural resources for the advancement of all of us.
I go now to Manitoba. In five years Manitoba had an influx of over 225 new industries. This is what Hon. Douglas L. Campbell had to say:
Unprecedented industrial expansion has taken place in the last few years. Manufacturing production in 1951 broke previous records and totalled an estimated $596 million. This represents over a 180 per cent increase over the 1941 total of $211,534,751. New records were also achieved in the number of employees which reached an estimated 44,700 with corresponding payrolls totalling an all-time high of over 100 million dollars.
Then I go on to another article dealing with immigration, which states that some
760,000	immigrants have come to Canada since the end of world war II. I cannot help but pay my compliments to the minister of immigration for making it possible for some of those people who have been flooded out in Holland to come to Canada with the least possible delay. I understand that already a few of them have landed on our shores. That fact will give great comfort to the many Dutch people who live in my district.
I come now to an article in this Monetary Times by Carl O. Nickle, the member for Calgary West, headed, "Oil Industry sets new records. $250 million spent in exploration." You will all recall how this hon. member fought the pipe line that was going to come to Winnipeg last year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He kept that pipe line back all one session.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On a question of privilege- Mr. Sinnott: I will say the whole Conservative party fought it, along with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruick-shank). And he had this to say:
Over the next few months it is hoped that plans will jell for a proposed major gas pipe line eastward from Alberta-a huge system reaching to Ontario and Quebec provided the economics are proved to be sound, or reaching to Winnipeg and then south into the U.S. mid-west should an allCanadian line not be feasible.
Well, he argued here for weeks that the route east would be feasible. At the present time the line has not been built as far as Winnipeg.
The British American Oil Company has this to say, that the operations of 1952 are much 
larger than ever before. Then Trans-Canada Air Lines reports a record for 1952 in the movement of passengers. Is that a sign of depression? I would not say so.	With
respect to chemical expansion we find this heading:	"Range of Chemical Production
Widens with Plant Expansions." Surely that shows that Canada is forging ahead.
Then we come to the Toronto stock exchange and the statement that the share volume approaches the 597 million mark, a record higher than ever before. A year ago, when all these stock exchanges could not handle the business, a new one was opened in Edmonton. And here is something to prove that the opposition is wrong: "Steady Increase in Deposits Banking Feature for 1952". The article following this heading states that while the deposits in 1951 reached the $9,000 million mark, in 1952 they reached $9,334 million.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the point?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The point is that the people still had more money to put into the banks last year than they had in the year before, despite what the hardware merchant has been soaking them. Then an article by H. S. Backus, president of the investment dealers' association of Canada has this heading: "Huge Capital Investment sparks Economic Expansion". The last article to which I shall refer bears this heading: "Life Insurance now in force Close to $19 Billion".
I suggest that these few phrases I have quoted from the businessmen of this country surely indicate the trend is for the better, not for the worse. Then, so far as our trade is concerned, all hon. members heard the report made to the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) upon his return from Latin America.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No; what did he say?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He said that the prospects for the future are very good, in the sense that our trade with Latin America has increased by 180 per cent since the war. He reported that there is also a great possibility of making sales of western wheat to Latin America.
Hon. members will recall the discussion that took place in the house last year with respect to what I described as the nuisance tax on radios. Speaking from this side of the house I pleaded with the government to repeal that tax.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And now we know why it was repealed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And I want to thank the government at this time for meeting that request.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now we know why it was done.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What do you want done next year, John?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now I come to a sore subject, the matter of railway wages and farm product prices.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What magazine is that in?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If you will come over here you can see my notes. But I don't suppose you could read them if you came over.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Your slip is showing, John. That's knocking them off.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The farmers in this country have borne the reduction in the cost of living, a cost that has been declining continuously for some time. No one can say that any other basic industry has borne one cent of that cost. It has been on the backs of the farmers, and the farmers alone. Yesterday's edition of the Ottawa Citizen contains this:
Farm wages were up about $1 a month on the average, and wages in other industry were up about $2.50 a week.
In non-farm industry, the average wage was $53.96 a week in early January, an increase from $50.42 a year earlier but down from $56.12 in December because of seasonally-lower employment.
On farms the average monthly wage was $87 with board and $122 without board, up $1 in each case from a year previously.
And this was in today's Journal:
Living costs as reflected by the new consumer price index dropped one-fifth of a point during January to 115-5 from 115.7, the bureau of statistics reported today. It was the third monthly decline in a row.
The January drop, propelled mostly by lower food prices, followed a decline of three-tenths of a point last November and one-tenth of a point in December.
That is with respect to food prices. I wonder who produces the food?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, go back to your magazine.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say the farmers produce the food. Then the article continues:
Under the new index, the food group dropped four-fifths of a point in January to 112.7 from 113-5.
I will not read further, because we all know that the cost of living index has been coming down for the last seven or eight months, and I must repeat that this burden has been borne by the farmers of Canada, and by them alone.
Hon. members will find on the order paper this resolution standing in my name:
That, in the opinion of this house, in view of the emergency now existing and the urgency of a program of war preparedness, the government should take into early consideration the advisability of introducing legislation to make strikes illegal for a period of two years, providing, at
The Budget-Mr. Sinnott the same time, for the settlement of labour disputes by arbitration between labour and management.
Today the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) asked whether the government would appoint a mediator to settle the strike at the Vancouver terminal. I think that would be a good move, and that the companies involved, the employees and the government should each appoint a man. If this were done the dispute could be settled very quickly, and at the same time it would keep the grain moving from western Canada.
I put this resolution on the order paper despite the fact-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With the full support of the government?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have heard a lot of bellowing from Souris tonight. I put it on the order paper because in spite of the fact that farm commodity prices were going down, railway employees were asking for a 35 per cent increase in wages, and I could not see any justification for it. And I have not heard the hon. member for Souris going to battle on behalf of the farmers because of the high freight rates they are charged.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You could find it in Hansard if you looked.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If we are to have a continuous spiral of wages we will have increased costs and the railways will have to ask for higher freight rates. The result will be that the consumers and farmers of Canada will have to pay for those higher costs through increased freight rates.
So I say the time has come when the upward spiral should cease, when wage earners should look at the picture with realism and understand that the farmers have taken a beating lately on account of the dropping prices. The wage earners should understand that they should accept some of that burden.

The first one is taken from the Financial Post of February 7, 1953. It is to be found in the column "The Nation's Business". The heading is, "Not Exactly Paupers These Railwaymen". It reads as follows:
Last week Canadian railwaymen got a 12 per cent boost in wages. That is the price the country had to pay to avoid a complete tie-up of the nation's main transportation lines. Even before that boost the people who operate our trains were hardly in the pauper class. Here are average
annual earnings:
Passenger engineers	$6,335
Freight engineers	 5,485
Passenger firemen	 4,860
Freight firemen	 3,670
Passenger conductors	 5,545
Freight conductors	 5,615
Baggagemen	 4,285
Passenger trainmen	 4,285
Freight trainmen	 3,790
Yardmen	 3,165
Sleeping car conductors	 3,780
Sleeping car porters	 2,940
Station agents	 3,710
Telephone operators	 2,725
Messengers, office boys, etc	2,300
And those, it should be remembered, are average wages. Men with more seniority and who, because of that seniority get the choicest runs, would do very much better. Some engineers on the passenger runs, for example, make as high as $8,000 a year, freight engineers $7,000 and conductors almost as much. The best trainmen's jobs will pay at least $1,800 a year above the average rate.
The national industrial conference board in the United States has calculated how much work it takes to buy food today compared with 1914. This is how it looks:
			1914	1952
hr.	min.	min.1	doz. eggs 	26	221	lb. bread 	17	61	qt. milk 	24	81	lb. coffee 	20	311	lb. round steak 	.... 1	2	40
As I have said, railway wages are high. Railway employees have asked for an increase in spite of the fact that farm prices have gone down. Some commodities have fallen as much as 30 per cent in the last two years. The reason I referred to the table of wages was for the purpose of disclosing and proving 

beyond a shadow of a doubt that there was no justification for a strike a short time ago. Costs of transportation, due largely to labour demands, have risen to the point where it is unbearable to think of further increases. In fact if labour were fair to their farmer friends they would take a hand in accepting a lower wage formula which would be in line with what farmers are being subjected to at the present time.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

The real farmer who produces butter, cheese, milk, eggs and all the primary products does not work an eight hour day or a forty hour week. Neither does he get three weeks' holidays with pay, a free pass on the railway, a free trip to the United States once a year, and he is not paid every two weeks. He gets paid for what he produces on a competitive market.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), or rather the member who lives in Ottawa and represents that constituency, has pretty well supported railway unions, as have the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and also the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher). The hon. member for Vancouver East, who made the statement some years ago that he had never hired a man and never would, has also been a great labour union man. They, in supporting labour unions and their consistent demands for higher wages-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: to the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott). I notice that in the speech he just made he and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) are poles apart. The hon. member for Springfield is wrong in most instances, but tonight he was right when he said that in the last two years many agricultural prices had fallen by some 30 per cent. The Minister of Agriculture this afternoon, and again this evening, attempted to prove that the farmer now is in a better position than ever before in the history of Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that statement by the minister can be borne out by the facts.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did not try to do anything of the kind.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What has actually happened is that during the war, since the war, and after Korea farm prices rose; but during the last year or two many farm prices have been falling rapidly and drastically. The minister was able to put on the record figures showing high cash farm income, not because farm prices have not gone down but merely because western Canada, during these two years, has had record crops by way of volume. Apparently the Minister of Agriculture is attempting to take credit even for the good rains, and the good crops we have had because of weather conditions.
The Minister of Agriculture spoke for over 40 minutes, his full time, but it was a different speech than he usually makes. I have not heard many full dress speeches by the Minister of Agriculture in which he has not pointed out the many advantages that would follow from the building of the South Saskatchewan river dam, but I notice the


minister stayed a long way away from that subject when he spoke this evening. It was the one thing he did not mention, but he has a new project now that he has been turned down on the South Saskatchewan dam. He brought this to light in a recent speech in Saskatchewan. He is now going to build a railroad, I believe from Churchill to Prince Rupert, right across the northern part of Canada where very few people live. It is not even going to skirt the mountains, as someone said. It is going to go right through. It is a very grand scheme, all in the mind of the Minister of Agriculture, as was the South Saskatchewan river dam about which he has spoken now for some 18 years.
I notice that he is attempting to turn the responsibility of the federal government for the prices of farm products going into interprovincial and export trade back to the various provincial governments. I notice that he pointed out that the Liberal provincial governments in Canada have pretty well failed to support farm prices, because he said that the province of Ontario had the best price support legislation.
I wonder why the party to which the minister belongs, after it replaced the Anderson government back in 1934 in the province of Saskatchewan, did not do something there, if that was the place to do it, in order to put floors under farm products prices in those days. Of course it would be just as nonsensical for me to say that the Liberal party in Saskatchewan in 1935 or 1936 should have placed floors under farm prices as it was for the minister this evening to say that it is a responsibility of the provincial governments.
The Minister of Agriculture might well take a lesson from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who has in his department the handling and marketing of grain; and the Minister of Trade and Commerce has in his department the wheat board. The wheat board establishes initial prices, and it controls the marketing of grain. The Minister of Trade and Commerce does not say that is the responsibility of the provinces. On behalf of the government he has accepted his responsibility, and that legislation is good. The legislation of the Minister of Agriculture, when it comes to the handling of farm products prices and setting adequate floor prices, has been a near total failure.
I notice that one thing the Minister of Agriculture did not talk about tonight was the situation in regard to the floor price under eggs. We have had floor prices of one kind or another before, but the floor price under beef has gone. This government is

expecting the United States government to establish floor prices for beef. However, the minister did not mention the floor price for eggs. The floor price is 38 cents for grade A large going into storage, with 5 cents per dozen being paid to the packers. That legislation, judging from the results, is wholly worthless. I have been receiving letters in the last few days and the last few weeks from farm women and people in my constituency, pointing out that they are now receiving for good, sound fresh eggs in the province of Saskatchewan the magnificent sum of 18 cents a dozen. That is the kind of floor price we have received from this Liberal government.
That is the way the Minister of Agriculture has dealt with floor prices on farm products. Those floor prices, as I have said, have been almost a total flop.
The Minister of Agriculture started out by saying that we have to compare the post-war years with years before the war; we cannot compare wartime years because things are abnormal. Then when he came to take two periods for comparison he took 1943-45 and 1949-51. In other words the minister will take the war years when those statistics suit his purpose, but when those statistics do not suit his purpose he says those are abnormal times. Then, to prove that this government is not too bad after all, he has to go back to the early thirties under a Conservative government. The thing that amazed me in the statistics he gave about prices was that during the Conservative regime the prices were so much better than prices during part of the time after the Liberal government took office.

The Budget-Mr. Argue Ottawa, with the present Minister of Agriculture as the minister of agriculture, the farmers in Saskatchewan were forced to sell many cattle for a cent a pound, $10 a head.

Then the minister said that the price of wheat under the Bennett government was terrible. Well, it was terrible. The minister said it averaged 60 cents a bushel. The price of wheat went up under the Liberal government to over a dollar a bushel. After the Minister of Agriculture had been here about three years the price went up to $1.45 right in Saskatchewan. However, the farmer was not selling the wheat; he was buying seed and he was charged $1.45 or $1.50 per bushel. Then he was asked to pay that money back the next fall, or any part of it that he could, when under this benevolent Liberal government the price of wheat to the farmer had fallen to 50 cents a bushel.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame, shame.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Under this Liberal government which has always been good to agriculture- so it says-if you got a bushel of seed wheat from them you had the privilege of paying it

The Budget-Mr. Argue back and of paying three bushels for every one you put in the ground.
Had the Minister of Agriculture been fair he would have pointed out that the statistical index covering costs and prices shows that the farm position today is worse than it has been at any time in the past ten years. The farmer's cost of production is going up and up, and the farmer's prices are going down and down. For the last year the minister has been telling the farmer to hold his cattle and feed them grain, that everything would be all right just as soon as the United States market was opened.
Well, the United States market is open, and I have not seen much improvement in cattle prices. The minister has been able to remove the floor from cattle prices, and he has gotten out of all responsibility. The best information we get from the men in his own depart-

ment is that cattle prices in the United States will go down by 20 per cent in the next four years. Under this government, of course, when United States cattle prices go down so do Canadian cattle prices. They have taken off the. floor, but even if they had a floor they would not pay the farmer. They would pay their friends in the packing industry, and then the farmer would have to try to get his money from that industry.
